title: Studies 2A–2C: Investment Evaluation
text:
For both our fictitious startups (Software: PerkSouq; Healthcare: Brachytix), we ran online experiments to determine how the (stated) likelihood to invest depends on the substantive quality and visual fluency of a pitch deck.
Specifically, we first ran a 2x2 between-subjects experiment for our software startup. To make sure that the instruction we used when measuring investment likelihood (“Based on the information at hand, what is the probability […]”) did not bias the results, we ran a replication of this first experiment with a modified instruction (“Based on the pitch deck, what is the probability […]”). To ensure generalizability across domains, we then ran the same experiment for our healthcare startup.
We ran all online experiments on Qualtrics, hosted the pitch decks on DocSend, and recruited the participants via Prolific. For details, see the corresponding AsPredicted preregistrations listed in Table 1.

In what follows, we will give an overview of the results and robustness checks, followed by figures that summarize the results of the experiments. As this report is dynamically created with R and Quarto, we also report all code. However, for readability, code is hidden by default and only the relevant results are shown.


Code
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')

# setup
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggsignif)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)
options(knitr.kable.NA = '',
        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - supernova
# - car
# - rstatix
# - forcats
# - weights
# - broom
# - scales
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - hrbrthemes
# - emmeans
# - grid


# Custom functions
#
# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# extract t-test results and Cohen's d and put the results together as a table
ttest_tbl <- function(formula, data, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # first, check for homogeneous group variances using Levene's test
  # --> if significant, use Welch's t-test (i.e., var.equal = FALSE)
  # note that we use a significance level of .05 for Levene's test, as preregistered
  # we check if the p-value is not significant (i.e., p >= .05) and save this
  # information var.equal --> thus, we can use 'var.equal = var.equal' in the t-test
  var.equal <- car::leveneTest(formula, data = data)$`Pr(>F)`[1] >= .05
  # perform t-test
  tres <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal, alternative = alternative)
  # extract Cohen's d
  dres <- rstatix::cohens_d(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal)
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3))
  # extract dependent variable
  dv <- stringr::str_match(deparse(formula), '[^ ~]*')
  # construct return df
  df = data.frame(DV = NA, condition=rep(NA, 2), N = NA, Mean = NA, SD = NA, test_statistic = NA, p = NA, d = NA)
  # fill values
  df$DV[1] <- stringr::str_to_sentence(dres$`.y.`)
  df$condition <- c(dres$group1, dres$group2)
  df$N <- c(dres$n1, dres$n2)
  df$Mean <- weights::rd(aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = mean)[,2], 2)
  df$SD <- weights::rd(aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = sd)[,2], 3)
  df$test_statistic[1] <- paste0("t(",
                                 ifelse(var.equal == TRUE, tres$parameter,
                                        weights::rd(tres$parameter, 1)),
                                 ") = ",
                                 sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic))
  df$p[1] <- pval
  df$d[1] <- weights::rd(dres$effsize, 2)
  return(df)
}
#
# extract ANOVA results including eta squared and put the results together as a table
# -Note: needs the supernova library installed
anova_tbl <- function(formula, data, type = 3, ...){
  # perform ANOVA
  d <- supernova::supernova(lm(as.formula(deparse(formula)), data = data), type = type)$tbl
  # check whether ANOVA is univariate or factorial
  univariate <- all(d$term %in% c("Model", "Error", "Total"))
  # get rows of interest
  if(univariate) {
    effect_rows <- d$term %notin% c("Error", "Total")
  } else {
    effect_rows <- d$term %notin% c("Model", "Error", "Total")
  }
  # extract key parameters
  effect <- d$term[effect_rows]
  SS <- round(d$SS[effect_rows], 2)
  df <- d$df[effect_rows]
  df_res <- d$df[d$term == "Error"]
  statistic <- round(d$F[effect_rows], 2)
  pval <- ifelse(d$p[effect_rows] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$p[effect_rows], 3))
  eta <- ifelse(d$PRE[effect_rows] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$PRE[effect_rows], 3))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(effect, SS, df, df_res, statistic, pval, eta))
}
# extract GLM results and put the results together as a table
glm_tbl <- function(model, coef_digits = 2, coef_bold = TRUE, p_threshold = 0.05, ...){
  # extract model parameters
  if("tobit" %in% class(model)){ # tobit model -> broom::tidy does not work
    res <- parameters::model_parameters(model)
    res <- res[c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "z", "p")]
    names(res) <- c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")
    # res[] <- lapply(res, function(x) { attributes(x) <- NULL; x })
  } else {
    res <- broom::tidy(model)
  }
  pvals <- res$p.value
  res$estimate <- sprintf(paste0("%.", coef_digits, "f"), res$estimate)
  res$std.error <- sprintf("%.3f", res$std.error)
  res$statistic <- sprintf("%.2f", res$statistic)
  # format p value
  res$p.value <- ifelse(res$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p.value, 3))
  # make estimates bold if below critical p value
  if(coef_bold){
    res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
  }
  # bind R2 and Adj. R2 to model parameters
  r2 <- performance::r2(model) # extract R2
  end <- nrow(res) + seq_len(length(r2))
  res[end,"term"] <- names(r2)
  res[end,"estimate"] <- weights::rd(unlist(r2), digits = 3)
  # return result
  return(res)
}

title: Studies 2A–2C: Investment Evaluation
text:
4.1 Main analyses
Table 5 shows for each experiment the results of a factorial ANOVA that models stated investment likelihood as a function of the visual fluency condition and the substantive quality condition. Note that type III sum of squares were used, and the proportional reduction in error is reported as effect size (ηp2 in the table).


Code
# combine data
d <- bind_rows(list(
  Software = d_sw,
  `Software Replication` = d_sw_repl,
  Healthcare = d_hc),
  .id = "Startup")

# convert Startup to factor, change order of levels
d$Startup <- factor(d$Startup,
                    levels = c("Software", "Software Replication", "Healthcare"),
                    labels = c("Software", "Software (replication)", "Healthcare"))

# convert conditions into factors
d$fluency <- as.factor(d$fluency)
d$quality <- as.factor(d$quality)

# relevel factor levels
d$quality <- relevel(d$quality, 'high')
d$fluency <- relevel(d$fluency, 'high')

# convert factor into effect coding
contrasts(d$fluency) <- contr.sum
contrasts(d$quality) <- contr.sum


# combine results
temp <- bind_rows(
  anova_tbl(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software")),
  anova_tbl(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)")),
  anova_tbl(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare"))
  )

temp |>

title: Studies 2A–2C: Investment Evaluation
text:
4.2 Manipulation checks
In this section, we report the results of the manipulation checks for visual fluency and substantive quality (software startup replication and healthcare startup experiments). We conducted t-tests for each manipulation check, with either processing ease or perceived venture quality as the dependent variable and the visual fluency condition or the substantive quality condition as independent variables. The results are shown in Table 6 (a) for processing ease and Table 6 (b) for perceived venture quality. Note that we ran either Student’s or Welch’s t-test based on the result of Levene’s test for homogeneous group variances. With the t-tests, we deviate from the preregistration of Study 2B, in which we erroneously wrote that we would run a two-factor ANOVA for the manipulation checks. We corrected this mistake in the preregistration of Study 2C.

bind_rows(
  ttest_tbl(fluency_perception ~ fluency, d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)")),
  ttest_tbl(fluency_perception ~ fluency, d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare"))
) |>
  mutate(DV = rep(c("Processing ease", ""), 2)) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Outcome", "Fluency Condition", "N", "Mean", "SD", "t-test", "p", "Cohen's d"), escape = FALSE) |>

title: Studies 2A–2C: Investment Evaluation
text:
4.3 Robustness checks
As a robustness check, we estimated linear regression models in which we predicted the stated investment likelihood by visual fluency, substantive quality, age, gender, investment experience and the centrality of visual product aesthetics (CVPA). In this regression, we again used effect coding for the two factors visual fluency and substantive quality. That is, for both variables, we coded low as -1 and high as +1. Table 7 shows the results of this regression.


Code
# -- Note: We comment out Levene's tests of homogeneous group variances here for
#          readability. However, we adapt the function call of the regression
#          based on the result of Levene's tests.


# Levene's test of homogeneous group variances -> if not, use robust::lmRob() below
#
# # software startup
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency, d |> filter(Startup == "Software")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software")) # not significant
# # software startup replication
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency, d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)")) # not significant
# # healthcare startup
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency, d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare")) # not significant
# car::leveneTest(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality, d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare")) # not significant

# recode Likert text scores into numeric values for the CVPA score
d |> mutate_at(vars(cvpa_v_1:cvpa_r_3), dplyr::recode,
                   'Strongly disagree' = 1,
                   'Disagree' = 2,
                   'Neither agree nor disagree' = 3,
                   'Agree' = 4,
                   'Strongly agree' = 5) -> d
# create CVPA composite score
d <- d |> rowwise() |> mutate(CVPA = mean(c_across(cvpa_v_1:cvpa_r_3))) |> ungroup()

# group "Non-binary" and "Prefer not to say" gender categories into one
d$gender <- forcats::fct_collapse(d$gender, Female = "Female", Male = "Male", other_level = "Other")

# run regression
glm_tbl(lm(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality + age + gender + invest_experience + CVPA,
             d |> filter(Startup == "Software"))) -> lm_rob_sw
glm_tbl(lm(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality + age + gender + invest_experience + CVPA,
             d |> filter(Startup == "Software (replication)"))) -> lm_rob_sw_repl
glm_tbl(lm(invest_prob ~ fluency * quality + age + gender + invest_experience + CVPA,
             d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare"))) -> lm_rob_hc

# add empty row for `genderOther` in the first and third regression
lm_rob_sw |> add_row(.before = 6)  -> lm_rob_sw
lm_rob_hc |> add_row(.before = 6)  -> lm_rob_hc


temp <- bind_cols(lm_rob_sw, lm_rob_sw_repl[,-1], lm_rob_hc[,-1]) |>
  mutate(term = c("Intercept", "Fluency", "Quality", "Age",
               "Gender [Male]", "Gender [Other]",
               "Investment experience", "CVPA",
               "Fluency × Quality", "R<sup>2</sup>", "R<sup>2</sup><sub>adj.</sub>")) |>
  arrange(term %notin% c("Intercept", "Fluency", "Quality", "Fluency × Quality"))
names(temp) <- c("", rep(c("Coeff.", "SE", "t", "p"), 3))
temp |>

title: LLM Ratings
text:
We used a panel of seven vision-capable large language models (LLMs) to check the manipulations of the pitch decks for Studies 3 and 4. For each of the eight fictitious startups of these studies (Servora, Curato, Ironhall, Foliant, Pulsegrid, Paperloom, Sentyl, and Axonmesh), there are four versions of the pitch deck that cross visual fluency (low vs. high) with substantive quality (low vs. high). The models rated the visual design and the substantive quality of all 32 pitch decks with the same items that the participants of our manipulation checks had answered. The panel also rated the pitch decks of these manipulation checks (Software: PerkSouq; Healthcare: Brachytix), which allows a comparison with the human participants’ ratings. In addition, we tested whether the rating differences remained when the text or the visual design of the pitch decks was removed. The panel’s quality ratings also determined the q-scores that we used for the incentives in Studies 3 and 4.
The text-based quality ratings of the real pitch decks are documented in the Deck Benchmarking Reproducibility Report. Note that these analyses were not preregistered.
In what follows, we will give an overview of the results, followed by figures that summarize the results. As this report is dynamically created with R and Quarto, we also report all code. However, for readability, code is hidden by default and only the relevant results are shown.


Code
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')

# setup
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)
options(knitr.kable.NA = '',
        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - weights
# - scales
# - hrbrthemes

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)


# Custom functions
#
# prepare the LLM panel ratings: numeric ratings and, for the original design
# items, simplicity as the reverse-coded complexity item (i.e., 8 - complexity)
# -Note: the complexity ratings are kept, the simplicity ratings are added
panel_prep <- function(d){
  d$rating <- as.numeric(d$rating)
  d_simplicity <- d |> filter(item == "complex") |> mutate(item = "simplicity", rating = 8 - rating)
  bind_rows(d, d_simplicity) |> filter(!is.na(rating))
}
#
# compare the high and the low condition of a factor at the level of the
# startups: mean rating per startup and condition (i.e., averaged across the
# models, the repetitions, and the two levels of the other factor), mean of the
# startup-level differences, percentile bootstrap 95% CI (4,000 resamples of the
# startups), Cohen's d_z, and the exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test
# -Note: since R 4.6.0, `wilcox.test` computes the exact (conditional) p-value
#        also in the case of tied differences (older versions of R use the
#        normal approximation in this case)
# -Note: if a margin is given, the result also contains the p-value of an
#        equivalence test (two one-sided t-tests, TOST) of the startup-level
#        differences against this margin
panel_contrast <- function(d, item, factor, high, low, margin = NA){
  # mean rating per startup and condition
  cells <- d[d$item == item & d[[factor]] %in% c(high, low), ] |>
    group_by(startup, level = .data[[factor]]) |>
    summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = level, values_from = rating) |>
    tidyr::drop_na()
  diffs <- cells[[high]] - cells[[low]]
  # percentile bootstrap 95% CI of the mean difference
  set.seed(0)
  boot <- replicate(4000, mean(sample(sort(diffs), replace = TRUE)))
  ci <- quantile(boot, c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
  # exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-sided)
  wres <- wilcox.test(cells[[high]], cells[[low]], paired = TRUE, exact = TRUE)
  # equivalence test (TOST)
  p_tost <- NA
  if(!is.na(margin)){
    p_tost <- max(t.test(diffs, mu = -margin, alternative = "greater")$p.value,
                  t.test(diffs, mu = margin, alternative = "less")$p.value)
  }
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(n = nrow(cells), high = mean(cells[[high]]), low = mean(cells[[low]]),
                    diff = mean(diffs), ci_low = ci[1], ci_high = ci[2],
                    d = mean(diffs) / sd(diffs), p = wres$p.value, margin = margin, p_tost = p_tost))
}
#
# format the results of `panel_contrast` for a table
panel_tbl <- function(res){
  data.frame(high = weights::rd(res$high, 2), low = weights::rd(res$low, 2),
             diff = weights::rd(res$diff, 2),
             CI = paste0("[", weights::rd(res$ci_low, 2), ", ", weights::rd(res$ci_high, 2), "]"),
             d = weights::rd(res$d, 2),
             p = ifelse(res$p < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p, 3)),
             margin = ifelse(is.na(res$margin), NA, paste0("±", res$margin)),
             p_tost = ifelse(is.na(res$p_tost), NA,
                             ifelse(res$p_tost < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p_tost, 3))))
}
#
# intraclass correlations of a matrix of ratings (rows = rated decks, columns =
# raters): two-way random effects and absolute agreement for a single rater,
# ICC(2,1), and for the mean of the k raters, ICC(2,k) (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979)
# -Note: rows with missing values are removed
icc_2 <- function(m){
  m <- as.matrix(m)
  m <- m[complete.cases(m), ]
  n <- nrow(m); k <- ncol(m); g <- mean(m)
  # mean squares of the rows (decks), the columns (raters), and the residuals
  ms_rows <- k * sum((rowMeans(m) - g)^2) / (n - 1)
  ms_cols <- n * sum((colMeans(m) - g)^2) / (k - 1)
  ms_error <- sum((m - outer(rowMeans(m), colMeans(m), "+") + g)^2) / ((n - 1) * (k - 1))
  # construct return vector
  return(c(icc_1 = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (k - 1) * ms_error + k * (ms_cols - ms_error) / n),
           icc_k = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (ms_cols - ms_error) / n)))
}
#
# quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa of two raters for the categories 1 to 7
# -Note: kappa is not defined (NA) if both raters give all decks the same rating
kappa_w <- function(a, b, categories = 1:7){
  obs <- table(factor(a, levels = categories), factor(b, levels = categories))
  expected <- outer(rowSums(obs), colSums(obs)) / sum(obs)
  weights <- outer(categories, categories, function(i, j) (i - j)^2) / (length(categories) - 1)^2
  if(sum(weights * expected) == 0) return(NA)
  return(1 - sum(weights * obs) / sum(weights * expected))
}
#
# agreement between the models of the LLM panel for a set of items: ICC(2,1) and
# ICC(2,k) of the scale mean per deck and model (i.e., the mean across the items
# and the three repetitions), and the quadratic-weighted kappa averaged across
# all pairs of models and across the items (per item, a model's three ratings of
# a deck are averaged and rounded)
panel_reliability <- function(d, items){
  # scale mean per deck and model
  m <- d |> filter(item %in% items) |>
    group_by(file, model) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rating) |>
    tidyr::drop_na()
  icc <- icc_2(m[, -1])
  # rounded mean rating per item, deck, and model
  r <- d |> filter(item %in% items) |>
    group_by(item, file, model) |>
    summarize(rating = pmin(pmax(round(mean(rating)), 1), 7), .groups = "drop")
  pairs <- combn(sort(unique(r$model)), 2)
  kappas <- unlist(lapply(items, function(it){
    w <- r |> filter(item == it) |> select(-item) |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rating) |> tidyr::drop_na()
    apply(pairs, 2, function(p) kappa_w(w[[p[1]]], w[[p[2]]]))
  }))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(decks = nrow(m), models = ncol(m) - 1, icc_1 = icc[["icc_1"]],
                    icc_k = icc[["icc_k"]], kappa = mean(kappas, na.rm = TRUE),
                    pairs_defined = sum(!is.na(kappas)), pairs = length(kappas)))
}
#
# repeat the column headers of a table above each group of rows (except the
# first), so that the headers are visible for every part of a long table
# -Note: the header rows of the HTML table are inserted before the rows with
#        the group labels (cf. `pack_rows`), without the stripes of the rows
repeat_header <- function(tbl){
  html <- as.character(tbl)
  header <- sub("(?s).*<thead>(.*)</thead>.*", "\\1", html, perl = TRUE)
  header <- gsub('<th style="', '<th style="box-shadow: none; ', header, fixed = TRUE)
  groups <- gregexpr('<tr grouplength=', html, fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  for(pos in rev(groups[-1])){
    html <- paste0(substr(html, 1, pos - 1), header, substr(html, pos, nchar(html)))
  }
  attributes(html) <- attributes(tbl)
  return(html)
}

title: LLM Ratings
text:
3.1 LLM panel and procedure
The panel consisted of seven vision-capable LLMs from seven developers (Table 1), which we accessed via OpenRouter between June 30 and July 1, 2026. In each call, a model received all slides of one pitch deck as images (JPEG, 2,000 pixels wide) together with one questionnaire, and it returned a rating and a one-sentence justification for each item. Every call was independent of all other calls. Each model rated each pitch deck three times per questionnaire, with a temperature of 0.1 and the reasoning effort set to high. The visual design and the substantive quality were rated in separate calls, and Section 5 shows the exact prompts.



Table 1: Overview LLM Panel





Model

MiniMax


Qwen3.7-plus
Alibaba






We used three questionnaires. The first two contain the original items of our human manipulation checks. The design questionnaire asks how clear, complex (reverse-coded as simplicity), rich in contrast, and symmetrical the visual design of the pitch deck is, and it contains the perceived venture quality item (the startup’s potential irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design). The quality questionnaire contains the perceived venture quality item and the four quality dimensions (commercialization opportunity, intellectual property, human capital, and organizational legitimacy). Both questionnaires end with the processing ease item (“The process of studying this pitch deck was …”, 0 = difficult to 100 = easy). All other items are rated on 1–7 scales. Since the models’ ratings of the original design items differed only little between the high and the low fluency versions (see Table 2), we added a third questionnaire with specific visual items. These items describe what a low and a high rating looks like, for example, symmetry as the left-right mirror balance of the slides (which is what the imagefluency symmetry score measures). This questionnaire also asks for the startup’s potential judged from the substance alone and for the processing ease of the pitch deck (0–100). It also contained an item on the overall visual polish, which has no counterpart in the human manipulation checks and is not analyzed here.
For the 32 pitch decks of Studies 3 and 4, the data contain ratings from 671 calls with the original design items, 669 calls with the original quality items, and 671 calls with the specific visual items (planned: 672 calls each). Across all questionnaires and sets of pitch decks (including the pitch decks of the manipulation checks and the modified pitch decks, see below), 3,018 of the 3,024 planned calls returned a complete set of valid ratings. The remaining 6 calls were not repeated.
Since the models act as raters rather than as independent observations, we analyzed the ratings at the level of the startups. For each startup and condition, we averaged the ratings across the models, the repetitions, and the two versions of the other factor (e.g., for the fluency manipulation, the high and the low quality version). The difference between the high and the low condition is the mean of the eight startup-level differences. We report the percentile bootstrap 95% confidence interval of this difference (4,000 resamples of the startups), Cohen’s dz, and the p-value of an exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the eight startup-level differences. Note that with only eight startups, this test cannot result in a p-value below .008. This smallest possible p-value results if the difference has the same sign for all eight startups, that is, if the high condition received higher (or lower) ratings than the low condition for every startup.

3.3 Separation of the two manipulations
Table 4 shows whether each manipulation also changed the ratings of the other construct, that is, whether the quality manipulation changed the ratings of the visual design and whether the fluency manipulation changed the ratings of the substantive quality. In addition to the tests of Table 2 and Table 3, the table reports equivalence tests (two one-sided t-tests, TOST, on the eight startup-level differences) with margins of ±0.5 rating points for the 1–7 items and ±5 points for processing ease (0–100). title: LLM Ratings
text:
3.4 Agreement between the models
Table 5 shows how closely the seven models agreed with each other. For each questionnaire, we averaged each model’s ratings of a pitch deck across the items and the three repetitions, which results in a matrix of 32 decks × 7 models. Based on this matrix, ICC(2,1) is the reliability of the ratings of a single model and ICC(2,k) is the reliability of the mean rating of all seven models (two-way random effects, absolute agreement). The weighted kappa is the quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ between two models, averaged across all 21 pairs of models and across the items of the questionnaire (per item, a model’s three ratings of a deck were averaged and rounded to the nearest scale point).

rel_flu <- panel_reliability(d_flu, c("clear", "contrast", "symmetrical", "simplicity"))
rel_vis <- panel_reliability(d_vis, c("clear", "contrast", "symmetrical", "simplicity"))
rel_qua <- panel_reliability(d_qua, c("overall", "commercialization", "ip", "management", "legitimacy"))

section: 3.5 Comparison with the human manipulation checks
text:
3.5 Comparison with the human manipulation checks
For the pitch decks of our manipulation checks, Table 6 compares the differences between the high and the low condition in the ratings of the human participants (see the Manipulation Checks Reproducibility Report) with those in the ratings of the LLM panel. The human participants each rated one pitch deck, and the models rated the same pitch decks with the same original items. Both the human and the LLM ratings are pooled across the software and the healthcare startup. Since there are only two startups per manipulation, we compare the direction of the differences only. Note also that these pitch decks were created in 2022 and might be part of the models’ training data.


Code
# mean ratings of the human participants per condition (pooled across both startups)
human_means <- function(y, group){
  c(high = mean(y[group == "high"], na.rm = TRUE), low = mean(y[group == "low"], na.rm = TRUE))
}
# mean ratings of the LLM panel per condition (pooled across both startups)
panel_means <- function(d, item, factor, high, low){
  c(high = mean(d$rating[d$item == item & d[[factor]] %in% high]),
    low = mean(d$rating[d$item == item & d[[factor]] %in% low]))
}

  # fluency manipulation
  human_means(d_mc_design$clarity, d_mc_design$fluency_condition),
  human_means(d_mc_design$contrast, d_mc_design$fluency_condition),

title: LLM Ratings
section: 3.6 Pitch decks without text or without visual design
text:
3.6 Pitch decks without text or without visual design
To test whether the models based their ratings of the visual design on the visual design and their ratings of the substantive quality on the text, we rendered two modified versions of the pitch decks of Studies 3 and 4. In the first, all text was made invisible, whereas the visual design was kept. We created this version for the 16 high quality decks (i.e., the high and the low fluency version of each startup), and the panel rated it with the original design items. In the second, the visual design was replaced by black text on a white background (without images or charts), whereas the text was kept. We created this version for the 16 high fluency decks (i.e., the high and the low quality version of each startup), and the panel rated it with the original quality items. For each item, Table 7 shows the difference between the high and the low condition (e.g., high minus low fluency) twice: for the complete decks (i.e., the ratings of Table 2 and Table 3, restricted to the same decks) and for the modified decks. If the models based their ratings of the visual design on the visual design only, removing the text should not change the difference between the high and the low fluency versions. Likewise, if they based their ratings of the substantive quality on the text only, removing the visual design should not change the difference between the high and the low quality versions.

Code
# complete decks: the same cells as the modified decks
d_flu_hq <- d_flu |> filter(quality == "HQ")
d_qua_hf <- d_qua |> filter(fluency == "HF")

  panel_contrast(d_flu_hq, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
  panel_contrast(d_flu_hq, "contrast", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
  panel_contrast(d_flu_hq, "symmetrical", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
  panel_contrast(d_flu_hq, "simplicity", "fluency", "HF", "LF")
)

  panel_contrast(d_flu_notext, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),

)
# quality manipulation: complete decks vs. decks without visual design
res_removal_qua_full <- bind_rows(
  panel_contrast(d_qua_hf, "overall", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
  panel_contrast(d_qua_hf, "commercialization", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
  panel_contrast(d_qua_hf, "ip", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),

title: LLM Ratings
text:
3.7 q-scores
The bonus in Studies 3 and 4 depended on the q-score of the startup that was drawn for the participant (see the Study 3: Attention and Investment Allocation Reproducibility Report and the Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease Reproducibility Report). The q-score of each startup and quality level is based on the panel’s ratings of the perceived venture quality item in the quality questionnaire (“Overall, the startup’s potential to generate a sustainable competitive advantage and positive returns to the stakeholders is …”). For each model, we averaged its ratings across the two fluency versions and the repetitions (three per deck, two for three combinations of model and deck). We then averaged the seven model means and rescaled the result to the range from 0 to 1, that is, q = (M − 1) / 6. Since the high and the low fluency version of a pitch deck share the same q-score, the q-scores reward substantive quality only. Table 8 shows the q-scores.


Code
# mean rating of the venture quality item per startup, quality level, and model,
# then mean across the seven models, rescaled to the range from 0 to 1
d_qua |> filter(item == "overall") |>
  group_by(startup, quality, model) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(startup, quality) |> summarize(q = (mean(rating) - 1) / 6, models = n(), .groups = "drop") -> q_scores

q_scores |> tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = startup, names_from = quality, values_from = q) |>
  mutate(startup = factor(startup_labels[startup], levels = startup_labels)) |>
  arrange(startup) |>
  mutate(diff = HQ - LQ) |>
  select(startup, HQ, LQ, diff) |>
  kbl(digits = 3, col.names = c("Startup", "High Quality", "Low Quality", "Difference"),
      align = "lccc") |>
  kable_styling() |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "q-Score" = 3))

Code
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')

# setup
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - rstatix
# - weights
# - stringr
# - readr
# - car
# - tidyr
# - hrbrthemes
# - grid

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)

# Custom functions
#
# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# extract t-test results and Cohen's d and put the results together as a string
ttest_str <- function(formula, data, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # first, check for homogeneous group variances using Levene's test
  # --> if significant, use Welch's t-test (i.e., var.equal = FALSE)
  # note that we use a significance level of .05 for Levene's test, as preregistered
  # we check if the p-value is not significant (i.e., p >= .05) and save this
  # information var.equal --> thus, we can use 'var.equal = var.equal' in the t-test
  var.equal <- car::leveneTest(formula, data = data)$`Pr(>F)`[1] >= .05
  # perform t-test
  tres <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal, alternative = alternative)
  # extract Cohen's d
  dres <- rstatix::cohens_d(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal)
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", paste0(" = ",weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3)))
  # extract dependent variable
  dv <- stringr::str_match(deparse(formula), '[^ ~]*')
  # construct return string
  return(paste0(stringr::str_to_sentence(dv),
                "\nt(",
                ifelse(var.equal == TRUE, tres$parameter, weights::rd(tres$parameter, 1)),
                ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic),
                ", p", pval,
                "; d = ", weights::rd(dres$effsize, 2)))
}
#
# extract t-test results and Cohen's d and put the results together as a table
ttest_tbl <- function(formula, data, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # first, check for homogeneous group variances using Levene's test
  # --> if significant, use Welch's t-test (i.e., var.equal = FALSE)
  # note that we use a significance level of .05 for Levene's test, as preregistered
  # we check if the p-value is not significant (i.e., p >= .05) and save this
  # information var.equal --> thus, we can use 'var.equal = var.equal' in the t-test
  var.equal <- car::leveneTest(formula, data = data)$`Pr(>F)`[1] >= .05
  # perform t-test
  tres <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal, alternative = alternative)
  # extract Cohen's d
  dres <- rstatix::cohens_d(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal)
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3))
  # extract dependent variable
  dv <- stringr::str_match(deparse(formula), '[^ ~]*')
  # construct return df
  df = data.frame(DV = NA, condition=rep(NA, 2), N = NA, Mean = NA, SD = NA, test_statistic = NA, p = NA, d = NA)
  # fill values
  df$DV[1] <- stringr::str_to_sentence(dres$`.y.`)
  df$condition <- c(dres$group1, dres$group2)
  df$N <- c(dres$n1, dres$n2)
  df$Mean <- weights::rd(aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = mean)[,2], 2)
  df$SD <- weights::rd(aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = sd)[,2], 3)
  df$test_statistic[1] <- paste0("t(",
                                 ifelse(var.equal == TRUE, tres$parameter,
                                        weights::rd(tres$parameter, 1)),
                                 ") = ",
                                 sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic))
  df$p[1] <- pval
  df$d[1] <- weights::rd(dres$effsize, 2)
  return(df)
}

title: Manipulation Checks
text:
4.1 Design manipulation (visual fluency)
In this between-subjects experiment, we presented participants one of two pitch decks that varied only in their visual fluency. The content (i.e., substantive quality) was held constant across conditions. Specifically, the pitch deck’s design was systematically varied by a design agency with the instruction that four dimensions of visual fluency (contrast, clarity, symmetry, simplicity) should be each either relatively high or relatively low. The goal was to create a high fluency and a low fluency pitch deck.
In the online experiment, participants were randomly assigned to one of the two visual fluency conditions, had to open and carefully study the pitch deck, and answer questions on their perceived contrast, clarity, simplicity, symmetry, processing ease, and perceived venture quality.
Of the 175 responses recorded in Qualtrics, 160 were finished, and 100 participants remained after the exclusions.

4.1.1 Results
Table 3 shows the results of all t-tests that were run. Each t-test compares the group means of the respective dependent variable across the two visual fluency conditions. Note that we ran either Student’s or Welch’s t-test based on the result of Levene’s test for homogeneous group variances.


Code
d <- design_sw

# convert fluency_condition to factor
d$fluency_condition <- as.factor(d$fluency_condition)

# -- Note: Although for most hypotheses a direction was specified, we do not
#          specify alternative = "greater" in our tests. However, we include
#          comments in the code where this would have been "allowed", so that
#          an interested reader can divide the resulting p-values by 2.

# 1. Contrast
res_contr <- ttest_tbl(contrast ~ fluency_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 2. Clarity
res_clar <- ttest_tbl(clarity ~ fluency_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 3. Symmetry
res_sym <- ttest_tbl(symmetry ~ fluency_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 4. Simplicity
res_simpl <- ttest_tbl(simplicity ~ fluency_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 5. Processing Ease
res_pf <- ttest_tbl(fluency ~ fluency_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 6. Venture Quality
res_qual <- ttest_tbl(quality ~ fluency_condition, data = d)

res_pf[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_pf[1,1], "Fluency", "Processing ease")
res_qual[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_qual[1,1], "Quality", "Perceived venture quality")

# put all results together
bind_rows(res_contr, res_clar, res_sym, res_simpl, res_pf, res_qual) |>

title: Manipulation Checks
text:
4.2 Quality manipulation
In this between-subjects experiment, we presented participants one of two pitch decks that varied only in their substantive quality. The design (i.e., visual fluency) was held constant across conditions. Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two substantive quality conditions, had to open and carefully study the pitch deck, and rate the startup’s intellectual property, human capital, commercialization opportunity, legitimacy, and perceived venture quality. They further had to rate the processing ease of the pitch deck.
Of the 194 responses recorded in Qualtrics, 172 were finished, and 113 participants remained after the exclusions.

4.2.1 Results
Table 4 shows the results of all t-tests that were run. Each t-test compares the group means of the respective dependent variable across the two quality conditions. Note that we ran either Student’s or Welch’s t-test based on the result of Levene’s test for homogeneous group variances.


Code
d <- quality_sw

# convert quality_condition to factor
d$quality_condition <- as.factor(d$quality_condition)

# -- Note: Although for most hypotheses a direction was specified, we do not
#          specify alternative = "greater" in our tests. However, we include
#          comments in the code where this would have been "allowed", so that
#          an interested reader can divide the resulting p-values by 2.

# 1. Intellectual Property
res_intell <- ttest_tbl(intell_prop ~ quality_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 2. Human Capital
res_hum <- ttest_tbl(hum_cap ~ quality_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 3. Commercialization opportunity
res_commerc <- ttest_tbl(commerc ~ quality_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 4. Organizational legitimacy
res_legitim <- ttest_tbl(legitim ~ quality_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 5. Overall Venture Quality / Potential
res_qual <- ttest_tbl(quality ~ quality_condition, data = d) # alternative = "greater"

# 6. Processing Ease
res_pf <- ttest_tbl(fluency ~ quality_condition, data = d)

res_intell[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_intell[1,1], "Intell_prop", "Intellectual property")
res_hum[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_hum[1,1], "Hum_cap", "Human capital")
res_commerc[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_commerc[1,1], "Commerc", "Commercialization opportunity")
res_legitim[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_legitim[1,1], "Legitim", "Organizational legitimacy")
res_qual[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_qual[1,1], "Quality", "Perceived venture quality")
res_pf[1,1] <- stringr::str_replace(res_pf[1,1], "Fluency", "Processing ease")

# put all results together

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
This report reproduces the results, tables, and figures of the paper and its appendix. Its sections follow the order of the paper, and its hypotheses, tables, and figures are numbered as in the paper and its appendix. Each section starts from the processed data of the respective study. The detailed reproducibility report of each study, linked at the beginning of each section, documents how the raw data were processed and which participants and observations were excluded, and it reports the full models and further analyses.
As this report is dynamically created with R and Quarto, we also report all code. However, for readability, code is hidden by default and only the relevant results are shown.


Code
# setup
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)
options(knitr.kable.NA = '',
        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - stringr
# - forcats
# - weights
# - scales
# - car
# - rstatix
# - supernova
# - afex
# - BayesFactor
# - lme4
# - lmerTest
# - performance
# - marginaleffects
# - AER
# - irr
# - hrbrthemes
# - ggsankey
# - purrr
# - grid

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)

# folders of the processed and the raw data
processed_dir <- 'reproducibility_reports/data'
raw_dir <- 'reproducibility_reports/data'

# colors
blue_main <- "#297FB8"
blue_dark <- "#2D3E50"
blue_light <- "#A0ABBF"


# Custom functions
#
# two decimals
f2 <- function(x) sprintf('%.2f', x)
#
# p-value in the text, e.g., "p = .663" or "p < .001"
p_txt <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "*p* < .001", paste0("*p* = ", weights::rd(p, 3)))
#
# p-value in a table
p_tbl <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", weights::rd(p, 3))
#
# 95% confidence interval, e.g., "[2.14, 5.73]"
ci_txt <- function(lower, upper) paste0("[", f2(lower), ", ", f2(upper), "]")
#
# format a Bayes factor (values above 1,000 in scientific notation,
# e.g., 1.16 × 10^4)
bf_fmt <- function(bf){
  ifelse(bf > 1000,
         paste0(sprintf('%.2f', bf / 10^floor(log10(bf))), " × 10<sup>", floor(log10(bf)), "</sup>"),
         sprintf('%.2f', bf))
}
#
# one-sample t-test of a participant-level contrast against zero: N, mean,
# two-sided 95% confidence interval, and p-value of the requested test
# -Note: NAs (participants without a valid contrast) are removed before the test
contrast_test <- function(x, alternative = "two.sided"){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  tres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = alternative)
  cres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
  data.frame(N = length(x), estimate = mean(x), lower = cres$conf.int[1],
             upper = cres$conf.int[2], p = tres$p.value)
}
#
# model-based difference between the high and the low condition in a
# mixed-effects model with effect coding (i.e., two times the coefficient),
# with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value (Satterthwaite's
# degrees of freedom)
lmer_diff <- function(model, term){
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[term, ]
  data.frame(estimate = 2 * fe[["Estimate"]],
             lower = 2 * (fe[["Estimate"]] - qt(.975, fe[["df"]]) * fe[["Std. Error"]]),
             upper = 2 * (fe[["Estimate"]] + qt(.975, fe[["df"]]) * fe[["Std. Error"]]),
             p = fe[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
}
#
# repeat the column headers above each row group of a table (`last_labels`:
# other labels above the last group, e.g., c("p" = "p (TOST)"))
repeat_header <- function(tbl, last_labels = NULL){
  html <- as.character(tbl)
  header <- sub("(?s).*<thead>(.*)</thead>.*", "\\1", html, perl = TRUE)
  header <- gsub('<th style="', '<th style="box-shadow: none; ', header, fixed = TRUE)
  groups <- gregexpr('<tr grouplength=', html, ignore.case = TRUE)[[1]]
  for(pos in rev(groups[-1])){
    h <- header
    if(pos == max(groups)) for(old in names(last_labels)){
      h <- sub(paste0(">\\s*", old, "\\s*<"), paste0(">", last_labels[[old]], "<"), h, perl = TRUE)
    }
    html <- paste0(substr(html, 1, pos - 1), h, substr(html, pos, nchar(html)))
  }
  attributes(html) <- attributes(tbl)
  return(html)
}
#
# two-sided independent-samples t-test of the high vs. the low condition (Welch's test
# if the median-centered Levene test is significant at .05) with Cohen's d
mc_ttest <- function(formula, data){
  # check for homogeneous group variances (Levene's test, centered at the median)
  var_equal <- car::leveneTest(formula, data = data)$`Pr(>F)`[1] >= .05
  # perform t-test and extract Cohen's d
  tres <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = var_equal)
  dres <- rstatix::cohens_d(formula, data = data, var.equal = var_equal)
  # condition means and SDs (high condition first)
  means <- aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = mean)[, 2]
  sds <- aggregate(formula, data = data, FUN = sd)[, 2]
  # construct return df (degrees of freedom of Welch's test with one decimal)
  data.frame(n_high = dres$n1, n_low = dres$n2, mean_high = means[1], mean_low = means[2],
             sd_high = sds[1], sd_low = sds[2], t = tres$statistic[["t"]],
             df_txt = ifelse(var_equal, as.character(tres$parameter[["df"]]), weights::rd(tres$parameter[["df"]], 1)),
             p = tres$p.value, d = dres$effsize[[1]])
}
#
# condition means and t-test in the text, e.g., "M_high = 66.27, M_low = 46.69,
# t(98) = 3.65, p < .001, d = .73"
mc_ttest_txt <- function(res){
  paste0("*M*<sub>high</sub> = ", f2(res$mean_high), ", *M*<sub>low</sub> = ", f2(res$mean_low),
         ", *t*(", res$df_txt, ") = ", f2(res$t), ", ", p_txt(res$p), ", *d* = ", weights::rd(res$d, 2))
}
#
# t-test as a figure label (outcome, t-test, p-value, and Cohen's d)
mc_ttest_str <- function(formula, data){
  res <- mc_ttest(formula, data)
  dv <- stringr::str_match(deparse(formula), '[^ ~]*')
  paste0(stringr::str_to_sentence(dv), "\nt(", res$df_txt, ") = ", f2(res$t),
         ", p", ifelse(res$p < .001, " < .001", paste0(" = ", weights::rd(res$p, 3))),
         "; d = ", weights::rd(res$d, 2))
}
#
# model-based difference between the high and the low condition in a linear
# model with effect coding (two times the coefficient, four times for an
# interaction), with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value
lm_diff <- function(model, term, multiplier = 2){
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[term, ]
  ci <- confint(model)[term, ]
  data.frame(estimate = multiplier * fe[["Estimate"]], lower = multiplier * ci[[1]],
             upper = multiplier * ci[[2]], p = fe[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
}
#
# type III ANOVA of a linear model: SS, df, residual df, F, p, and partial eta
# squared of each effect
anova_3 <- function(model){
  tbl <- supernova::supernova(model, type = 3)$tbl
  effects <- !(tbl$term %in% c("Model", "Error", "Total"))
  data.frame(SS = tbl$SS[effects], df = tbl$df[effects], df_res = tbl$df[tbl$term == "Error"],
             F = tbl$F[effects], p = tbl$p[effects], eta = tbl$PRE[effects])
}
#
# t-test of the high vs. the low condition (factor levels "high", "low"; Student's
# or Welch's test, depending on Levene's test): means, difference, 95% CI, t, df, p
ttest_diff <- function(formula, data){
  var.equal <- car::leveneTest(formula, data = data)$`Pr(>F)`[1] >= .05
  tres <- t.test(formula, data = data, var.equal = var.equal)
  data.frame(low = tres$estimate[[2]], high = tres$estimate[[1]],
             estimate = tres$estimate[[1]] - tres$estimate[[2]],
             lower = tres$conf.int[1], upper = tres$conf.int[2],
             t = tres$statistic[[1]], df = tres$parameter[[1]], p = tres$p.value)
}
#
# coefficients (estimate, SE, t, p) of the given terms of a linear model,
# followed by R² and adjusted R², formatted for a table
lm_tbl <- function(model, terms, labels){
  cf <- coef(summary(model))[terms, , drop = FALSE]
  data.frame(Term = c(labels, "R<sup>2</sup>", "R<sup>2</sup><sub>adj.</sub>"),
             Coeff = c(f2(cf[, "Estimate"]), weights::rd(summary(model)$r.squared, 3),
                       weights::rd(summary(model)$adj.r.squared, 3)),
             SE = c(sprintf('%.3f', cf[, "Std. Error"]), "", ""),
             t = c(f2(cf[, "t value"]), "", ""),
             p = c(p_tbl(cf[, "Pr(>|t|)"]), "", ""))
}
#
# prepare the LLM ratings: numeric ratings and, for the items of the human
# visual questionnaire, simplicity as the reverse-coded complexity item (8 - complexity)
llm_prep <- function(d){
  d$rating <- as.numeric(d$rating)
  d_simplicity <- d |> filter(item == "complex") |> mutate(item = "simplicity", rating = 8 - rating)
  bind_rows(d, d_simplicity) |> filter(!is.na(rating))
}
#
# high vs. low condition of a factor at the level of the startups: condition means
# (across models, repetitions, and the other factor), mean of the startup-level
# differences, percentile bootstrap 95% CI (4,000 resamples), Cohen's d_z, and the
# exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test
# -Note: since R 4.6.0, the exact p-value is also computed for tied differences
llm_contrast <- function(d, item, factor, high, low){
  # mean rating per startup and condition
  cells <- d[d$item == item & d[[factor]] %in% c(high, low), ] |>
    group_by(startup, level = .data[[factor]]) |>
    summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = level, values_from = rating) |>
    tidyr::drop_na()
  diffs <- cells[[high]] - cells[[low]]
  # percentile bootstrap 95% CI of the mean difference
  set.seed(0)
  boot <- replicate(4000, mean(sample(sort(diffs), replace = TRUE)))
  ci <- quantile(boot, c(.025, .975), names = FALSE)
  # exact Wilcoxon signed-rank test (two-sided)
  wres <- wilcox.test(cells[[high]], cells[[low]], paired = TRUE, exact = TRUE)
  # construct return df
  data.frame(n = nrow(cells), high = mean(cells[[high]]), low = mean(cells[[low]]),
             estimate = mean(diffs), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2],
             d = mean(diffs) / sd(diffs), p = wres$p.value)
}
#
# intraclass correlations of a matrix of ratings (rows = rated decks, columns =
# raters): ICC(2,1) and ICC(2,k), two-way random effects, absolute agreement
llm_icc <- function(m){
  m <- as.matrix(m)
  m <- m[complete.cases(m), ]
  n <- nrow(m); k <- ncol(m); g <- mean(m)
  # mean squares of the rows (decks), the columns (raters), and the residuals
  ms_rows <- k * sum((rowMeans(m) - g)^2) / (n - 1)
  ms_cols <- n * sum((colMeans(m) - g)^2) / (k - 1)
  ms_error <- sum((m - outer(rowMeans(m), colMeans(m), "+") + g)^2) / ((n - 1) * (k - 1))
  # construct return vector
  c(icc_1 = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (k - 1) * ms_error + k * (ms_cols - ms_error) / n),
    icc_k = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (ms_cols - ms_error) / n))
}
#
# quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa of two raters for the categories 1 to 7 (NA if
# both raters give all decks the same rating)
llm_kappa <- function(a, b, categories = 1:7){
  obs <- table(factor(a, levels = categories), factor(b, levels = categories))
  expected <- outer(rowSums(obs), colSums(obs)) / sum(obs)
  weights <- outer(categories, categories, function(i, j) (i - j)^2) / (length(categories) - 1)^2
  if(sum(weights * expected) == 0) return(NA)
  1 - sum(weights * obs) / sum(weights * expected)
}
#
# agreement between the models for a set of items: ICC(2,1) and ICC(2,k) of the
# scale mean per deck and model, and the weighted kappa averaged across all pairs
# of models and the items (per item, a model's three ratings are averaged and rounded)
llm_reliability <- function(d, items){
  # scale mean per deck and model
  m <- d |> filter(item %in% items) |>
    group_by(file, model) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rating) |>
    tidyr::drop_na()
  icc <- llm_icc(m[, -1])
  # rounded mean rating per item, deck, and model
  r <- d |> filter(item %in% items) |>
    group_by(item, file, model) |>
    summarize(rating = pmin(pmax(round(mean(rating)), 1), 7), .groups = "drop")
  pairs <- combn(sort(unique(r$model)), 2)
  kappas <- unlist(lapply(items, function(it){
    w <- r |> filter(item == it) |> select(-item) |>
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = rating) |> tidyr::drop_na()
    apply(pairs, 2, function(p) llm_kappa(w[[p[1]]], w[[p[2]]]))
  }))
  # construct return df
  data.frame(decks = nrow(m), models = ncol(m) - 1, icc_1 = icc[["icc_1"]],
             icc_k = icc[["icc_k"]], kappa = mean(kappas, na.rm = TRUE),
             pairs = length(kappas), undefined = sum(is.na(kappas)))
}
#
# three decimals, e.g., "-0.421"
bm_f3 <- function(x) sprintf('%.3f', x)
#
# 95% confidence interval with three decimals, e.g., "[-0.515, -0.328]"
bm_ci3 <- function(lower, upper) paste0("[", bm_f3(lower), ", ", bm_f3(upper), "]")
#
# correlation with three decimals and without a leading zero, e.g., ".153"
bm_r <- function(x) weights::rd(x, 3)
#
# 95% confidence interval of a correlation, e.g., "[.121, .186]"
bm_ci_r <- function(lower, upper) paste0("[", bm_r(lower), ", ", bm_r(upper), "]")
#
# Pearson correlation with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value
bm_cor <- function(x, y){
  res <- cor.test(x, y)
  data.frame(r = res$estimate[["cor"]], lower = res$conf.int[1], upper = res$conf.int[2], p = res$p.value)
}
#
# range of the ratings across the three prompt versions (per deck)
bm_prompt_range <- function(d, cols){
  apply(d[, cols], 1, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
}
#
# Welch two-sample t-test (first minus second group): N of both groups, mean
# difference, two-sided 95% confidence interval, and p-value of the requested
# test
# -Note: NAs (participants without a valid contrast) are removed before the test
welch_test <- function(x, y, alternative = "two.sided"){
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  tres <- t.test(x, y, alternative = alternative, var.equal = FALSE)
  cres <- t.test(x, y, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = FALSE)
  data.frame(N_1 = length(x), N_2 = length(y), estimate = mean(x) - mean(y),
             lower = cres$conf.int[1], upper = cres$conf.int[2], p = tres$p.value)
}
#
# difference implied by a coefficient of a mixed-effects model with effect
# coding (multiplier times the coefficient, i.e., 4 for a two-way and 8 for a
# three-way interaction), with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided
# p-value (Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom)
lmer_multi <- function(model, term, multiplier){
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[term, ]
  data.frame(estimate = multiplier * fe[["Estimate"]],
             lower = multiplier * (fe[["Estimate"]] - qt(.975, fe[["df"]]) * fe[["Std. Error"]]),
             upper = multiplier * (fe[["Estimate"]] + qt(.975, fe[["df"]]) * fe[["Std. Error"]]),
             p = fe[["Pr(>|t|)"]])
}
#
# odds ratio (high vs. low) of a factor with effect coding in a mixed logistic
# regression (i.e., exp(2 × coefficient)), with its 95% Wald confidence
# interval and two-sided p-value
glmer_or <- function(model, term){
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[term, ]
  data.frame(estimate = exp(2 * fe[["Estimate"]]),
             lower = exp(2 * (fe[["Estimate"]] - qnorm(.975) * fe[["Std. Error"]])),
             upper = exp(2 * (fe[["Estimate"]] + qnorm(.975) * fe[["Std. Error"]])),
             p = fe[["Pr(>|z|)"]])
}
#
# preregistered analysis of the fluency contrast in the disclosure condition
# (x): N, mean, 95% confidence interval, two-sided p-value, Bayes factor
# (Cauchy prior, r = 0.707), 90% confidence interval, p-value of the
# equivalence test (the larger p-value of the two one-sided tests against
# -bound and +bound), p-value of the Welch comparison with the control
# condition (x_control, two-sided), and case (1 to 5) and outcome of the
# preregistered decision rule
h4_tests <- function(x, x_control, bound = 0.225){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  x_control <- x_control[!is.na(x_control)]
  # two-sided test against zero, 90% confidence interval, and Bayes factor
  tres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
  ci90 <- t.test(x, mu = 0, conf.level = .90)$conf.int
  bf10 <- BayesFactor::extractBF(BayesFactor::ttestBF(x = x, mu = 0, rscale = 0.707))$bf
  # equivalence test (two one-sided tests)
  p_tost <- max(t.test(x, mu = -bound, alternative = "greater")$p.value,
                t.test(x, mu = bound, alternative = "less")$p.value)
  # control vs. disclosure (Welch t-test, two-sided)
  cres <- t.test(x_control, x, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = FALSE)
  # decision rule (cases in the preregistered order)
  est <- mean(x)
  case <- case_when(tres$p.value < .05 & est <= -bound ~ 1,
                    tres$p.value < .05 & est >= bound ~ 2,
                    p_tost < .05 & cres$p.value < .05 & mean(x_control) > est ~ 3,
                    tres$p.value < .05 & est > 0 & p_tost >= .05 ~ 4,
                    TRUE ~ 5)
  outcome <- c("overcorrection", "persistence supported", "switched off",
               "reduced but present", "indeterminate")[case]
  data.frame(N = length(x), estimate = est, lower = tres$conf.int[1], upper = tres$conf.int[2],
             p = tres$p.value, bf10 = bf10, lower_90 = ci90[1], upper_90 = ci90[2],
             p_tost = p_tost, p_control = cres$p.value, case = case, outcome = outcome)
}
#
# coefficients of a linear, logit, or Tobit model with standard errors, 95%
# confidence intervals (t-based for linear models, Wald otherwise), test
# statistics, and two-sided p-values
reg_coefs <- function(model){
  est <- coef(summary(model))
  est <- est[rownames(est) != "Log(scale)", , drop = FALSE]
  if(inherits(model, c("glm", "tobit"))) crit <- qnorm(.975) else crit <- qt(.975, model$df.residual)
  data.frame(term = rownames(est), estimate = est[, 1], se = est[, 2],
             lower = est[, 1] - crit * est[, 2], upper = est[, 1] + crit * est[, 2],
             statistic = est[, 3], p = est[, 4], row.names = NULL)
}
#
# k times a model coefficient (e.g., the high-minus-low contrast of an
# effect-coded factor) with its 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value;
# for logit models, the result is exponentiated (odds ratio)
coef_contrast <- function(model, term, k){
  res <- reg_coefs(model)
  res <- res[res$term == term, ]
  out <- data.frame(estimate = k * res$estimate, lower = k * res$lower, upper = k * res$upper,
                    statistic = res$statistic, p = res$p)
  if(inherits(model, "glm")) out[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")] <- exp(out[c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
  return(out)
}
#
# high-minus-low difference of the model-based probabilities of `variable`
# (balanced grid, equal weights over the other factors) in percentage points,
# with its delta-method 95% confidence interval and two-sided p-value; `by` and
# `hypothesis` as in marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()
pp_contrast <- function(model, variable, by = TRUE, hypothesis = NULL){
  res <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(model, variables = setNames(list(c("low", "high")), variable),
                                          by = by, hypothesis = hypothesis, type = "response",
                                          newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(model = model, grid_type = "balanced"))
  data.frame(estimate = 100 * res$estimate, lower = 100 * res$conf.low, upper = 100 * res$conf.high,
             statistic = res$statistic, p = res$p.value)
}
#
# coefficient rows of a regression table, with the terms relabeled and ordered
# as in `labels` (named vector) and estimates with `digits` decimals
coef_rows <- function(model, labels, digits = 2){
  res <- reg_coefs(model)
  res <- res[match(names(labels), res$term), ]
  fmt <- paste0('%.', digits, 'f')
  data.frame(Term = unname(labels), Estimate = sprintf(fmt, res$estimate), SE = sprintf('%.3f', res$se),
             CI = paste0("[", sprintf(fmt, res$lower), ", ", sprintf(fmt, res$upper), "]"),
             Statistic = f2(res$statistic), p = p_tbl(res$p))
}
#
# count with its percentage of n, e.g., "331 (7.4%)"
n_pct <- function(x, n) paste0(scales::comma(x), " (", sprintf('%.1f', 100 * x / n), "%)")
#
# mean with its standard deviation, e.g., "1.84 (3.80)"
mean_sd <- function(x) paste0(f2(mean(x)), " (", f2(sd(x)), ")")

title: Reproducibility Report
section: 3.1 Human manipulation checks: design and samples
text:
3.1 Human manipulation checks: design and samples
The human manipulation checks were four preregistered online experiments, one for each manipulation (visual fluency or substantive quality) and each startup of Studies 1 and 2 (the software startup PerkSouq and the healthcare startup Brachytix). Each experiment had a one-factor between-subjects design with random assignment to a high or a low condition. In the two visual checks, the decks differed in visual fluency and contained the same substantive information. In the two quality checks, they differed in substantive quality and had the same neutral design. The surveys ran on Qualtrics, the decks were hosted on DocSend, and the participants were recruited through Prolific.
Qualtrics recorded 175 responses in the software visual check, 194 in the software quality check, 187 in the healthcare visual check, and 188 in the healthcare quality check, of which 160, 172, 167, and 168 were finished. After the exclusions, 100 participants remained in the software visual check (49 high and 51 low fluency), 113 in the software quality check (56 high and 57 low quality), 104 in the healthcare visual check (52 high and 52 low fluency), and 108 in the healthcare quality check (66 high and 42 low quality). The analyses therefore included 425 participants. In all four checks, the exclusions also removed participants whose conditions recorded by Qualtrics and by DocSend disagreed, a rule that was not preregistered.
The mean age of the participants was 43.29 years in the software visual check, 41.05 years in the software quality check, 41.56 years in the healthcare visual check, and 41.30 years in the healthcare quality check. The share of women was 46.0%, 42.5%, 60.6%, and 45.4%, respectively.

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
3.2 Human manipulation checks: preregistered t-tests
The visual checks measured perceived contrast, clarity, symmetry, and complexity on scales from 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much), with complexity reverse-coded as simplicity (8 minus the response). They further measured processing ease, the overall fluency measure, with the item “The process of studying this pitch deck was …” on a scale from 0 (difficult) to 100 (easy), and perceived venture quality on a scale from 1 (very poor) to 7 (excellent). The quality checks measured intellectual property (organizational capital), human capital, commercialization opportunity, organizational legitimacy, and perceived venture quality on scales from 1 (very poor) to 7 (excellent), followed by the same processing-ease item. The preregistrations predicted higher ratings in the high condition for the first five outcomes of each check and no difference in perceived venture quality (visual checks) or processing ease (quality checks). As preregistered, each outcome was compared between the high and the low condition with an independent-samples t-test at α = .05, using Welch’s test when the median-centered Levene test indicated unequal variances (α = .05). All tests are two-sided, and Cohen’s d is the standardized difference between the high and the low condition. Table A1 reports the visual checks and Table A2 the quality checks. Figures A2, A3, A4, and A5 show the individual ratings and condition means of the four checks.
Results. In both visual checks, the high-fluency deck received higher ratings of contrast, clarity, and symmetry (all p < .001) and higher processing ease (software startup: Mhigh = 66.27, Mlow = 46.69, t(98) = 3.65, p < .001, d = .73; healthcare startup: Mhigh = 53.08, Mlow = 41.62, t(97.8) = 2.09, p = .040, d = .41). Perceived simplicity did not differ significantly (software startup p = .974, healthcare startup p = .551), and visual fluency did not significantly affect perceived venture quality (software startup: Mhigh = 4.94, Mlow = 4.61, t(98) = 1.50, p = .136, d = .30; healthcare startup: Mhigh = 5.25, Mlow = 5.12, t(102) = 0.73, p = .469, d = .14).
In the software quality check, the high-quality deck received higher ratings of intellectual property, human capital, organizational legitimacy, and perceived venture quality (largest p = .008). Perceived venture quality was 4.80 in the high-quality and 4.21 in the low-quality condition (t(111) = 2.82, p = .006, d = .53). Commercialization opportunity did not differ significantly (p = .227). In the healthcare quality check, the high-quality deck received higher ratings on all four substantive dimensions and perceived venture quality (largest p = .005). Perceived venture quality was 5.39 in the high-quality and 4.86 in the low-quality condition (t(106) = 2.87, p = .005, d = .57). Substantive quality did not significantly affect processing ease (software startup: Mhigh = 54.39, Mlow = 47.12, t(111) = 1.42, p = .158, d = .27; healthcare startup: Mhigh = 46.67, Mlow = 51.76, t(106) = -0.96, p = .338, d = -.19).

mc_d <- mc_design_sw

3.3 LLM checks of the pitch decks
The LLM ratings, the prompts, and further analyses are documented in the LLM Ratings Reproducibility Report.

# LLM checks of the pitch decks (not preregistered)
#
# ratings (one row per call and item), pitch decks of Studies 3 and 4: items of
# the human visual and quality questionnaires and the additional visual questions
llm_flu <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_Studies_3_4_Decks_Fluency_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
llm_qua <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_Studies_3_4_Decks_Quality_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
llm_vis <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_Studies_3_4_Decks_Specific_Visual_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
# single-factor decks of the manipulation checks
llm_flu_mc <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_MC_Decks_Fluency_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
llm_qua_mc <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_MC_Decks_Quality_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
llm_vis_mc <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_MC_Decks_Specific_Visual_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
# modified decks: text removed (visual questionnaire) and visual design removed
# (quality questionnaire)
llm_flu_notext <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_Text_Removed_Fluency_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
llm_qua_nodesign <- readr::read_csv(here(raw_dir, 'LLM_Panel_Design_Removed_Quality_Items.csv')) |> llm_prep()
# human manipulation checks (processed data), pooled across both startups
llm_mc_design <- bind_rows(readr::read_csv(here(processed_dir, 'MC_1_Design_Software.csv')),
                           readr::read_csv(here(processed_dir, 'MC_3_Design_Healthcare.csv')))
llm_mc_quality <- bind_rows(readr::read_csv(here(processed_dir, 'MC_2_Quality_Software.csv')),
                            readr::read_csv(here(processed_dir, 'MC_4_Quality_Healthcare.csv')))

                      "google/gemini-3.5-flash" = "Gemini 3.5 Flash",

                      "qwen/qwen3.7-plus" = "Qwen3.7-plus")

# retained calls (complete set of valid ratings) and planned calls (decks x 7
# models x 3 repetitions) per questionnaire and deck set
llm_calls_retained <- c(nrow(distinct(llm_flu, file, model, rep)), nrow(distinct(llm_qua, file, model, rep)),
                        nrow(distinct(llm_vis, file, model, rep)), nrow(distinct(llm_flu_mc, file, model, rep)),
                        nrow(distinct(llm_qua_mc, file, model, rep)), nrow(distinct(llm_vis_mc, file, model, rep)),
                        nrow(distinct(llm_flu_notext, file, model, rep)), nrow(distinct(llm_qua_nodesign, file, model, rep)))
llm_calls_planned <- c(n_distinct(llm_flu$file), n_distinct(llm_qua$file), n_distinct(llm_vis$file),
                       n_distinct(llm_flu_mc$file), n_distinct(llm_qua_mc$file), n_distinct(llm_vis_mc$file),
                       n_distinct(llm_flu_notext$file), n_distinct(llm_qua_nodesign$file)) * 7 * 3
llm_calls_missing <- llm_calls_planned - llm_calls_retained

# human questionnaire: visual fluency on the visual items and substantive
# quality on the quality items
llm_res_flu <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_flu, "contrast", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                         llm_contrast(llm_flu, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                         llm_contrast(llm_flu, "symmetrical", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),

           mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "management" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "HQ"]),
           mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "commercialization" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "HQ"]),
           mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "legitimacy" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "HQ"]),
           mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "overall" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "HQ"]),
           mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "ease" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "HQ"])),
  low = c(mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "contrast" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "clear" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "symmetrical" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "simplicity" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "ease" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_flu_mc$rating[llm_flu_mc$item == "potential" & llm_flu_mc$fluency == "LF"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "ip" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "management" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "commercialization" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "legitimacy" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "overall" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]),
          mean(llm_qua_mc$rating[llm_qua_mc$item == "ease" & llm_qua_mc$quality == "LQ"]))
)
llm_human$diff <- llm_human$high - llm_human$low
llm_models$diff <- llm_models$high - llm_models$low

# agreement between the seven models (pitch decks of Studies 3 and 4): mean of
# the four visual items and mean of the five quality items
llm_rel_flu <- llm_reliability(llm_flu, c("contrast", "clear", "symmetrical", "simplicity"))
llm_rel_qua <- llm_reliability(llm_qua, c("ip", "management", "commercialization", "legitimacy", "overall"))

# additional visual questions: visual fluency on the four visual items and the
# venture potential item, substantive quality on the revised ease item
llm_res_vis <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_vis, "contrast", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                         llm_contrast(llm_vis, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                         llm_contrast(llm_vis, "symmetrical", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                         llm_contrast(llm_vis, "simplicity", "fluency", "HF", "LF"))
llm_vis_potential <- llm_contrast(llm_vis, "potential", "fluency", "HF", "LF")
llm_vis_ease_quality <- llm_contrast(llm_vis, "ease", "quality", "HQ", "LQ")

# removal checks: complete decks (same decks as the modified decks) vs. decks
# without text (visual items, high quality decks) and decks in plain formatting
# (quality items, high fluency decks)
llm_flu_hq <- llm_flu |> filter(quality == "HQ")
llm_qua_hf <- llm_qua |> filter(fluency == "HF")
llm_removal_flu_full <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_flu_hq, "contrast", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_flu_hq, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_flu_hq, "symmetrical", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_flu_hq, "simplicity", "fluency", "HF", "LF"))
llm_removal_flu <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_flu_notext, "contrast", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_flu_notext, "clear", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_flu_notext, "symmetrical", "fluency", "HF", "LF"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_flu_notext, "simplicity", "fluency", "HF", "LF"))
llm_removal_qua_full <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_qua_hf, "ip", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_qua_hf, "management", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_qua_hf, "commercialization", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_qua_hf, "legitimacy", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                                  llm_contrast(llm_qua_hf, "overall", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"))
llm_removal_qua <- bind_rows(llm_contrast(llm_qua_nodesign, "ip", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_qua_nodesign, "management", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_qua_nodesign, "commercialization", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_qua_nodesign, "legitimacy", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"),
                             llm_contrast(llm_qua_nodesign, "overall", "quality", "HQ", "LQ"))
# difference for the decks in plain formatting as a percentage of the difference
# for the complete decks
llm_retained_qua <- llm_removal_qua$estimate / llm_removal_qua_full$estimate * 100

# substantive-quality scores (q-scores) of Studies 3 and 4 (AsPredicted
# Preregistration #304145): mean of the perceived venture quality item per startup,
# quality level, and model, then mean across the seven models, rescaled to 0-1
llm_qscores <- llm_qua |> filter(item == "overall") |>
  group_by(startup, quality, model) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(startup, quality) |> summarize(q = (mean(rating) - 1) / 6, models = n(), .groups = "drop")
llm_qscores_wide <- llm_qscores |> tidyr::pivot_wider(id_cols = startup, names_from = quality, values_from = q)
llm_qscores_wide$diff <- llm_qscores_wide$HQ - llm_qscores_wide$LQ


Note: The following analysis was not preregistered. For the pitch decks of Studies 3 and 4 (the four versions of each of the eight AI startups), we extended the manipulation checks with seven vision-capable large language models (LLMs) from different developers, accessed through OpenRouter: Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash, MiniMax M3, Qwen3.7-plus, MiMo V2.5, and Kimi K2.6. In each call, a model received all slides of one deck as images together with either the visual or the quality questionnaire of the human manipulation checks (same items and response scales) and returned a rating and a brief reference to supporting slide content for each item. Simplicity is the reverse-coded complexity rating. Each model rated each deck three times per questionnaire. The models also rated the 8 single-factor decks of the manipulation checks for Studies 1 and 2, which allows a direct comparison with the human ratings. Across these questionnaires, the additional visual questions, and the removal checks (see Section 3.4), 3,018 of the 3,024 planned calls returned a complete set of valid ratings. The other 6 calls failed or returned incomplete ratings (decks of Studies 3 and 4 with the human visual questionnaire: 1, with the quality questionnaire: 3, with the additional visual questions: 1, and decks without text: 1).
For each item and startup, we averaged the ratings across the models, the repetitions, and the two versions of the other manipulated factor, which gives a high and a low condition mean per startup. The difference between the conditions is the mean of the eight startup-level differences, reported with a percentile bootstrap 95% confidence interval (4,000 resamples of the startups), the paired standardized effect (Cohen’s dz), and the p-value of an exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Thus, the startups are the units of analysis, and the repeated model ratings are not treated as independent observations. With eight startups, the smallest possible p-value of this test is .008, which results if the difference has the same sign for all eight startups. Table A3, Panel A reports the effects of each manipulation on the items it targeted, and Panel B its effects on the items of the other construct. For the single-factor decks, Panel C compares the condition means of the models with those of the human participants, both pooled across the software and the healthcare startup. The reliability of the ratings of the 32 decks of Studies 3 and 4 (Panel D) is based on the mean of the four visual items and the mean of the five quality items per deck and model. ICC(2,1) is the reliability of a single model and ICC(2,7) that of the average of the seven models (two-way random effects, absolute agreement). The weighted κ is the quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ between two models, averaged across the 21 pairs of models and across the items (per item, a model’s three ratings of a deck were averaged and rounded). The 0–100 processing-ease item is not part of these means.
Results. Across the eight AI startups, high-fluency decks received higher ratings of contrast, clarity, symmetry, simplicity, and processing ease (all p = .008). Processing ease averaged 87.51 for high-fluency and 84.20 for low-fluency decks, a difference of 3.31 points (95% CI [2.85, 3.78]). High-quality decks received higher ratings on all four substantive dimensions and perceived venture quality (all p = .008). Perceived venture quality averaged 6.00 versus 3.42, a difference of 2.58 points (95% CI [2.44, 2.72]). The effects on the ratings of the other construct were smaller: substantive quality changed the four visual ratings by 0.02 to 0.20 points, and visual fluency changed the five quality ratings by -0.01 to 0.04 points. In the visual questionnaire, the effect of visual fluency on the separate perceived venture quality item was 0.01 points (95% CI [-0.04, 0.07], p = .742). Substantive quality also increased the processing-ease ratings in the quality questionnaire by 2.01 points (95% CI [1.59, 2.40], p = .008), so the models’ processing-ease ratings responded to substantive content as well as to visual design.
On the single-factor decks, the models, like the human participants, rated the high-fluency versions as easier to process and the high-quality versions as substantively stronger (Table A3, Panel C). The direction of the difference agreed in 11 of the 12 comparisons, with the perceived venture quality item of the visual questionnaire as the exception, and the models’ differences were mostly larger than the human participants’. The reliability of the seven-model average was .909 for visual design and .990 for substantive quality (ICC(2,7)). The corresponding single-model ICCs were .589 and .934, and the mean pairwise weighted κ values were .285 and .867 (Table A3, Panel D).
