title: Reproducibility Report
section: 3.4 Additional visual questions and removal checks
text:
3.4 Additional visual questions and removal checks
Note: The following analysis was not preregistered. The models also rated the 32 decks of Studies 3 and 4 with a later questionnaire of more specific visual questions (labeled “specific visual items” in Figure A6): legibility of the text (clarity), color and tonal strength (contrast), left-right balance (symmetry), and clutter on the visual surface (simplicity), each on a 1–7 scale with described anchors, a revised ease question that focuses on taking in the deck visually (0–100), and the venture’s potential judged from the substance alone. These questions form a separate instrument and do not replace the results using the human questionnaire. To assess what the ratings reflected, the models also rated two modified versions of the decks: the 16 high-quality decks with all readable text removed and the visual design kept (human visual questionnaire), and the 16 high-fluency decks in plain formatting with the text kept (quality questionnaire). Each comparison used the same complete decks as its baseline. All tests are those of Table A3. The complete item results, the reliability of the later questions, and the matched contrasts of the removal checks are in the LLM Ratings Reproducibility Report.
Results. With the later questions, high-fluency decks received higher ratings on all four visual features (differences from 1.20 to 3.22 points, all p = .008). The small venture-potential difference was also significant (0.09 points, 95% CI [0.04, 0.16], p = .031), and substantive quality increased the revised ease rating (3.10 points, 95% CI [1.72, 4.51], p = .008). After text removal, the differences in contrast (1.45 points, p = .008), clarity (0.49, p = .039), and simplicity (0.21, p = .008) remained significant, whereas the symmetry difference weakened from 0.77 points for the complete decks to 0.34 points and was no longer significant (95% CI [-0.01, 0.65], p = .109). With plain formatting, all five substantive-quality differences remained significant (all p = .008) and were essentially unchanged in magnitude (97% to 101% of the differences for the complete decks). Figure A6 shows the ratings of each model, using the later visual questions and the quality questionnaire.



Code
# aesthetics
#
# colors of the high and the low condition: the main blue and a burnt orange as
# its complementary color
llm_col_high <- blue_main
llm_col_low <- "#D4772C"

# theme settings
llm_theme <- theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
                   panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
                   plot.title = element_markdown(size = 13, family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", hjust = 0),
                   strip.text = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5),
                   axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5, margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 0, l = 0)),
                   axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10.5),
                   legend.position = "bottom")

# data prep
#
# mean rating per model, startup, item, and condition (i.e., across the two
# decks of a startup and condition and the three repetitions)
llm_fig_vis <- llm_vis |>
  filter(item %in% c("ease", "clear", "contrast", "symmetrical", "simplicity")) |>
  group_by(model, startup, item, level = fluency) |>
  summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop")
llm_fig_qua <- llm_qua |>
  filter(item %in% c("overall", "commercialization", "ip", "management", "legitimacy")) |>
  group_by(model, startup, item, level = quality) |>
  summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop")
# labels
llm_fig_vis$item <- factor(llm_fig_vis$item, levels = c("ease", "clear", "contrast", "symmetrical", "simplicity"),
                           labels = c("Processing ease\n(0–100)", "Clarity", "Contrast", "Symmetry", "Simplicity"))
llm_fig_qua$item <- factor(llm_fig_qua$item, levels = c("overall", "commercialization", "ip", "management", "legitimacy"),
                           labels = c("Perceived venture quality", "Commercialization\nopportunity", "Intellectual\nproperty",
                                      "Human capital", "Organizational\nlegitimacy"))
llm_fig_vis$level <- factor(llm_fig_vis$level, levels = c("HF", "LF"), labels = c("High", "Low"))
llm_fig_qua$level <- factor(llm_fig_qua$level, levels = c("HQ", "LQ"), labels = c("High", "Low"))
# models in alphabetical order (from top to bottom)
llm_fig_vis$model <- factor(llm_model_labels[llm_fig_vis$model], levels = rev(llm_model_labels))
llm_fig_qua$model <- factor(llm_model_labels[llm_fig_qua$model], levels = rev(llm_model_labels))
# means per model and condition
llm_fig_vis |> group_by(model, item, level) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") -> llm_fig_vis_means
llm_fig_qua |> group_by(model, item, level) |> summarize(rating = mean(rating), .groups = "drop") -> llm_fig_qua_means
# scale limits (processing ease: 0-100; all other items: 1-7)
llm_fig_vis_limits <- data.frame(item = factor(rep(levels(llm_fig_vis$item), each = 2), levels = levels(llm_fig_vis$item)),

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
3.5 Substantive-quality scores
The LLM Ratings Reproducibility Report lists the score of each startup and quality level.
Studies 3 and 4 used a common substantive-quality score (q-score) to determine the performance bonuses. For each of the eight startups at each quality level, we averaged the perceived venture quality item of the quality questionnaire across both visual versions and the repetitions within each model (three per deck, two for three combinations of model and deck). We then averaged the seven model means and rescaled the result from the 1–7 scale to the range from 0 to 1, that is, q = (M − 1) / 6. This construction was preregistered for Study 3 (AsPredicted #304145), and Study 4 reused the same scores (AsPredicted #309446).
Results. The 16 scores ranged from .341 to .845, and each is based on all 7 models. Each startup’s high-quality version had a higher score than its low-quality version (differences from .389 to .484). Since each score averages across both visual versions, the high- and the low-fluency version of a deck received the same score, so the score rewarded identifying the stronger substantive case without a direct payoff advantage for visual design.

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
4.1 Visual benchmark
We compared the 40 experimental pitch decks (the 8 versions of the software and the healthcare startup of Studies 1 and 2 and the 32 versions of the eight AI startups of Studies 3 and 4) with 3,510 real pitch decks submitted to a European VC firm focused on seed-stage investment. To maintain confidentiality, the firm computed the contrast, simplicity, and symmetry of its decks with an R script that uses the imagefluency package (Mayer, 2024), and the same measures were computed for the experimental decks. The deck-level scores are the means across the slides of a deck. For each measure, the percentile rank of an experimental deck is the percentage of real decks with a score at or below its score, and we report the median percentile rank of the high- and the low-fluency versions.
Results. All experimental decks lay within the observed ranges of the real decks on all three measures (contrast: .077 to .282, simplicity: .813 to .974, symmetry: .010 to .777). The high-fluency versions had median percentile ranks of 82.4 (contrast), 80.6 (simplicity), and 86.0 (symmetry), and the low-fluency versions had medians of 19.0, 13.2, and 16.8. Figure B1 shows the positions of all experimental decks and the median of each fluency condition.



Code
# aesthetics
#
# colors of high and low fluency: the main blue and a burnt orange as its
# complementary color
bm_col_high <- blue_main
bm_col_low <- "#D4772C"

# data prep
#
# long format of the real pitch decks
bm_bench_long <- bm_bench |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(contrast, simplicity, symmetry), names_to = "measure", values_to = "score")
bm_bench_long$measure <- factor(bm_bench_long$measure, levels = c("contrast", "simplicity", "symmetry"),
                                labels = c("Contrast", "Simplicity", "Symmetry"))
# mean of the real pitch decks
bm_bench_long |> group_by(measure) |> summarize(score = mean(score)) -> bm_bench_mean
# experimental pitch decks (rows: 1 = real decks, 2 = low fluency, 3 = high fluency)
bm_decks_fig <- bm_decks_long
bm_decks_fig$measure <- factor(bm_decks_fig$measure, levels = c("contrast", "simplicity", "symmetry"),
                               labels = c("Contrast", "Simplicity", "Symmetry"))
bm_decks_fig$row <- ifelse(bm_decks_fig$fluency == "HF", 3.3, 2.2)
bm_decks_fig$level <- factor(bm_decks_fig$fluency, levels = c("HF", "LF"), labels = c("High", "Low"))
bm_decks_fig$set <- factor(bm_decks_fig$set, levels = c("Studies 1 and 2", "Studies 3 and 4"),
                           labels = c("Decks of Studies 1 and 2", "Decks of Studies 3 and 4"))
# median score and percentile rank per measure and fluency version
bm_decks_fig |> group_by(measure, row) |>
  summarize(score = median(score), pr = median(pr), .groups = "drop") -> bm_decks_medians

# plot

  geom_violin(data = bm_bench_long, aes(x = score, y = 1), fill = "gray80", color = NA,
              orientation = "y", width = .9) +
  geom_segment(data = bm_bench_mean, aes(x = score, xend = score, y = .45, yend = 3.75),
               color = "gray45", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_text(data = bm_bench_mean, aes(x = score, y = .35, label = "mean"), size = 3.3,

             color = "gray15", stroke = .3, position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = .15, seed = 42)) +
  geom_segment(data = bm_decks_medians, aes(x = score, xend = score, y = row - .3, yend = row + .3),
               color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_label(data = bm_decks_medians, aes(x = score, y = row + .5, label = paste0("median: p", sprintf('%.0f', pr))),
             size = 3.3, family = "Roboto Condensed", color = "gray15", fill = "white", linewidth = 0,
             label.padding = unit(.1, "lines")) +
  facet_wrap(vars(measure), ncol = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2.2, 3.3), labels = c("Real pitch decks\n(3,510)", "Low fluency\nversions",
                                                         "High fluency\nversions"),
                     limits = c(.25, 3.95)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("High" = bm_col_high, "Low" = bm_col_low), guide = "none") +

        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

        plot.caption = element_markdown(hjust = 0, lineheight = 1.2, family = "Roboto Condensed", size = 10, margin = margin(t = 7, r = 0, b = 0, l = 0))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
4.2 Text-based substantive-quality measurement
We assessed the substantive evidence in the same 3,510 real decks separately from their visual design. The pipeline, which ran within the firm’s environment, rendered the slides as images, extracted their text with GLM-OCR, and replaced company names, founder names, and locations with placeholders (spaCy). Two open-weight models from different developers, Qwen 3.5 and Mistral 3 Large, then rated the anonymized text on 1–7 scales whose anchors described the evidence associated with low, intermediate, and high ratings: organizational capital (documented intellectual property and certifications), human capital, commercialization opportunity, organizational legitimacy, and a separate overall quality item. Each model rated each dimension of each deck with three meaning-preserving versions of the prompt, which results in 105,300 ratings (3,510 decks × 5 dimensions × 3 prompt versions × 2 models). Of these responses, 526 (0.5%) did not contain a rating (“I cannot determine”) and were replaced by the median of the available ratings of the same model, dimension, and prompt version. For each model and dimension, each prompt version was standardized across the decks, and the mean of the three standardized ratings was rescaled with the mean and the population standard deviation of all ratings of the model and dimension, bounded to the range from 1 to 7, and rounded to two decimals. The dimension score is the mean of the two model-level scores (rounded to two decimals), and the text-based quality score is the mean of the four standardized dimension scores (i.e., without overall quality). Correspondingly, the image-based fluency score is the mean of the standardized contrast, simplicity, and symmetry scores. Table B1 reports the scoring consistency for every dimension, including overall quality: the agreement across the three prompt versions (ICC(2,1), separately for each model), the agreement between the two models (quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ of their rounded model-level scores), and the prompt sensitivity (the percentage of decks for which the three ratings of at least one model differ by two or more points).
Results. Agreement across the prompt versions ranged from .876 to .902, and agreement between the models from .844 to .924. The ratings of at least one model differed by two or more points across the prompt versions for 24.1% of the decks for organizational capital, 18.4% for human capital, 25.5% for commercialization opportunity, 13.0% for organizational legitimacy, and 15.1% for overall quality. Thus, the ratings were generally consistent, while some assessments, in particular of organizational capital and commercialization opportunity, remained sensitive to the wording of the prompt.

           flip = paste0(sprintf('%.1f', bm_flip), "%")) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Dimension", "Qwen 3.5", "Mistral 3 Large", "Between models", "Prompt sensitivity"),
      caption = "Table B1: Scoring consistency and prompt sensitivity", align = "lcccc", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling() |>

  column_spec(1:5, extra_css = "white-space: nowrap;", include_thead = TRUE)

title: Reproducibility Report
section: 4.3 Relationship between visual fluency and substantive evidence
text:
4.3 Relationship between visual fluency and substantive evidence
We correlated the image-based fluency score with the text-based quality score and each of the three visual features with each of the four dimension scores (Pearson correlations). Top-quality decks are the 878 decks in the highest quartile of the text-based quality score. Figure B2 relates the two scores (left panel) and shows the distribution of all top-quality decks across the deciles of the fluency score (right panel, the bars add up to 100%). Table B2 reports, for each quartile of the fluency score, the mean text-based quality score (standardized across all decks) and the number and share of top-quality decks among the decks of the quartile.
Results. The image-based fluency score was weakly positively correlated with the text-based quality score (r = .153, 95% CI [.121, .186], p < .001), which corresponds to 2.4% shared variance. Correlations between the individual visual features and the four quality dimensions ranged from .041 to .095. Among the decks in the lowest fluency quartile, 178 of 878 (20.3%) were top-quality decks. The corresponding share in the highest fluency quartile was 289 of 878 (32.9%). Viewed from the other direction, 41.8% of the top-quality decks had fluency scores below the median of all decks (Figure B2, right panel). Thus, highly rated substantive evidence frequently appeared in less fluent decks, while the two scores remained positively associated.



Code
# data prep
#
# share of all top quality decks per fluency decile (in %)
bm_d |> filter(quality_top) |> count(fluency_decile) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n) * 100,
         below_median = factor(fluency_decile <= 5, levels = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                               labels = c("Below the median", "Above the median"))) -> bm_deciles
# correlation (for the label)
bm_r_label <- paste0("r = ", weights::rd(cor(bm_d$fluency_score, bm_d$quality_score), 3), " [",
                     weights::rd(cor.test(bm_d$fluency_score, bm_d$quality_score)$conf.int[1], 3), ", ",
                     weights::rd(cor.test(bm_d$fluency_score, bm_d$quality_score)$conf.int[2], 3), "]")

# figure: scatter plot
bm_ortho_1 <- ggplot(bm_d, aes(x = fluency_score, y = quality_score)) +
  geom_point(size = .9, alpha = .25, color = "gray45") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = blue_main, linewidth = .8, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE, color = blue_dark, fill = blue_light, linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("label", x = min(bm_d$fluency_score), y = max(bm_d$quality_score), label = bm_r_label, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 4, color = "gray15", fill = "white", linewidth = 0, family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum_rc() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_markdown(size = 13, family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", hjust = 0),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5, margin = margin(t = 0, r = 10, b = 0, l = 0)),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5, margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 0, l = 0))) +
  labs(x = "Image-based fluency score", y = "Text-based quality score",
       title = "<b>Fluency and quality</b> (all decks)")

# figure: top quality decks per fluency decile
bm_ortho_2 <- ggplot(bm_deciles, aes(x = factor(fluency_decile), y = share, fill = below_median)) +
  geom_col(width = .8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray45", linewidth = .5) +
  # shares as labels inside the bars
  geom_text(aes(y = 1, label = sprintf("%.1f%%", share), color = below_median), vjust = 0, size = 3.6,
            family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  annotate("text", x = .5, y = 10.3, label = "expected if unrelated (10%)", hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.5,
           color = "gray45", family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  # bracket over the deciles below the median
  annotate("segment", x = .6, xend = 5.4, y = 13, yend = 13, color = "gray45", linewidth = .5) +
  annotate("segment", x = c(.6, 5.4), xend = c(.6, 5.4), y = 13, yend = 12.5, color = "gray45", linewidth = .5) +
  annotate("text", x = .6, y = 13.3, label = paste0("below the median: ", sprintf('%.1f', sum(bm_deciles$share[bm_deciles$fluency_decile <= 5])),
                                                   "% of the top quality decks"),
           hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.6, color = "gray25", family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Below the median" = bm_col_low, "Above the median" = bm_col_high), name = "Fluency score:") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Below the median" = "gray15", "Above the median" = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1), limits = c(0, 16), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum_rc() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top",
        plot.title = element_markdown(size = 13, family = "Roboto Condensed", face = "plain", hjust = 0),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5, margin = margin(t = 0, r = 10, b = 0, l = 0)),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11, hjust = .5, margin = margin(t = 5, r = 0, b = 0, l = 0))) +

       title = "<b>Top quality decks</b> by fluency decile")

                     "Right: top quality decks = highest quartile of the<br>text-based quality score (n = ", sum(bm_d$quality_top),
                     "). The bars add up to 100%, and ", sprintf('%.1f', mean(bm_d$fluency_below_median[bm_d$quality_top]) * 100),

text:
4.4 Founder characteristics
We related the fluency score to the rated human-capital evidence (Pearson correlation) and regressed it on four characteristics that the VC firm recorded, in a linear regression (OLS): whether a founder had previously exited a venture (prior exit), serial-founder status, the prior funding raised (log-transformed, i.e., log(1 + x)), and the number of slides of the deck (Table B3).
Results. The correlation of the fluency score with the rated human-capital evidence was small (r = .116, 95% CI [.083, .149]). The four characteristics explained 2.3% of the variation in the fluency score after adjustment for the number of predictors (adjusted R2). Serial-founder status was positively associated with the score (b = 0.188, p < .001), whereas a prior exit was negatively associated with it (b = -0.421, p < .001). Neither the prior funding nor the number of slides had a significant conditional association (p = .471 and p = .626).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
4.5 Venture outcomes
The VC firm also recorded whether a startup received follow-on funding, whether it survived, and whether it had an exit through an IPO or an acquisition, together with whether the partner firm had funded the startup. Follow-on funding is a separate outcome from funding by the partner firm. We correlated both scores with each outcome (Table B4, Panel A) and estimated one joint logistic regression per outcome with both scores and funding by the partner firm as predictors (Panel B), with 95% profile-likelihood confidence intervals.
Results. Of the 3,510 decks, 599 were associated with funding by the partner firm and 2,911 were not. Both scores were positively associated with all three outcomes. The correlations with follow-on funding, survival, and exit were .235, .190, and .128 for the image-based fluency score and .104, .073, and .076 for the text-based quality score (all p < .001). In the joint models, the fluency score remained positively associated with follow-on funding (b = 0.747), survival (b = 0.629), and exit (b = 0.430, all p < .001). The quality score retained a positive association with follow-on funding (b = 0.130, p = .029), whereas its conditional associations with survival (b = 0.091, p = .117) and exit (b = 0.115, p = .109) were not significant.

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
5.1 Sample
The pitch emails were sent to 24,961 software investors and 15,016 healthcare investors. Of these, 3,809 and 1,681 emails were returned as hard bounces (for example, because an address was no longer valid), so that 21,152 and 13,335 emails were delivered, reaching 34,487 investors. Investors entered the sample if they clicked the link to the deck within 21 days of receiving the email, and only their activity within 21 days after the first click was analyzed. Viewing sessions flagged by DocSend as an “Atypical Source Visit”, sessions without an identifier, and sessions with an identifier outside the outreach sample were removed. 4,891 software investors and 2,480 healthcare investors had an eligible first click, corresponding to 23.1% and 18.6% of the delivered emails. Investors whose cumulative opening duration was below 3 seconds or above 30 minutes were then excluded. The analysis samples comprise the remaining 4,445 software and 2,408 healthcare investors (the retained deck viewers), 21.0% and 18.1% of the delivered emails. Table C1, Panel A gives the delivered emails and the retained deck viewers per condition, and Panel B describes the retained deck viewers. Figures C1 and C2 show the flow from the sent emails to the replies as Sankey diagrams.
Two independent raters, blind to the hypotheses, classified all 1,125 software and 761 healthcare email replies as to whether they demonstrated investor interest. Their agreement was 97.16% for the software startup (Cohen’s κ = .939) and 96.45% for the healthcare startup (κ = .919). The authors resolved the cases in which the raters disagreed. Only replies within 21 days after the first click count as positive reactions, and investors without such a reply are coded 0.

# define custom geom
s1_geom_sankey_label_richtext <- function (mapping = NULL, data = NULL, position = "identity",
  na.rm = FALSE, show.legend = NA, space = NULL, type = "sankey", width = 0.1,
  inherit.aes = TRUE, family =
    if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") "Roboto Condensed" else "Roboto Condensed Light", ...)  # added font family
{
  label.aes <- list(...)
  list(label = ggplot2::layer(stat = ggsankey:::StatSankeyText, data = data,
    mapping = mapping, geom = "richtext", position = position, # changed: geom = "label"
    show.legend = show.legend, inherit.aes = inherit.aes,
    params = purrr::flatten(list(na.rm = na.rm, width = width,
      space = space, type = type, label.aes, family = family))))
}

# change ipsum theme to work for sankey plot
s1_theme_sankey_ipsum_rc <- function (base_family = "Roboto Condensed", base_size = 11.5, ...)
{
  {
    hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum_rc(base_family = base_family, base_size = base_size, ...) %+replace%
      ggplot2::theme(panel.border = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "black",
          linewidth = ggplot2::rel(1)), legend.key = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        strip.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = "white",
          colour = "transparent", linewidth = ggplot2::rel(2)),
        complete = TRUE, axis.line.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.line.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        # set background to white for quarto to avoid transparency issues
        panel.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill='white', color='white'),
        plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill='white', color='white')
      )
  }
}

# create binary indicators for the different stages
s1_sankey_sw |> mutate(
  `Sent mails` = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 1 ~ "Hard bounce",
    hard_bounce == 0 ~ "Delivered"
  ),
  Delivered = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 0 & is.na(date_first_click) ~ "Recipient did not open deck",
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_first_click) ~ "Recipient opened deck"
  ),
  `Recipient opened deck` = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_first_click) & is.na(date_reply) ~ "Recipient did not reply",
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_reply) ~ "Recipient replied"
  ),
  `Recipient replied` = case_when(
    positive == 0 ~ "Negative reply",
    positive == 1 ~ "Positive reply"
  ),
  Category = category,
  `Initial sample` = "Software<br>startup"
) -> s1_sankey_sw

# make data long for sankey graph
s1_sankey_sw |> ggsankey::make_long(`Initial sample`, `Sent mails`, Delivered,
                                    `Recipient opened deck`, `Recipient replied`,
                                    Category) -> s1_df

# add group_nodes (needed for calculation of group percentages later)
s1_df |> mutate(
  group_node = case_when(
    node == "Hard bounce" | node == "Delivered" ~ "Software<br>startup",
    node == "Recipient did not open deck" | node == "Recipient opened deck" ~ "Delivered",
    node == "Recipient did not reply" | node == "Recipient replied" ~ "Recipient opened deck",
    node == "Negative reply" | node == "Positive reply" ~ "Recipient replied",
    node == "other" | node == "geography" | node == "no investments" | node == "stage" | node == "investment strategy" | node == "industry" | node == "no specific reason" ~ "Negative reply",
    node == "more info/clarification" | node == "meeting" | node == "formal application" | node == "updates" | node == "referral" ~ "Positive reply"
  )
) -> s1_df

# add information about node N and group_node N and calculate percentages
s1_df |>
  # count obs per node
  group_by(node) |> mutate(n = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # count obs per group_node
  group_by(group_node) |> mutate(n_group = ifelse(is.na(group_node), NA, n())) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # add percentages
  mutate(pct = n/n_group) -> s1_df

s1_df |> mutate(
  node = factor(node,
                levels = c("Software<br>startup",

# make sankey plot
#
# first change the data so that percentages are displayed in the node texts
s1_df |> tidyr::drop_na(node) |>
  mutate(
    pct = ifelse(is.na(pct), 9999, pct), # dummy-replace NA with 9999, otherwise later ifelse does not work
    node_text = ifelse(
      # group_node and thus pct empty (here: 9999)
      pct == 9999,
      # yes, pct empty -> no percentages
      sprintf("<span style='font-weight:bold; font-family:Roboto Condensed'>%s</span><br><span style='color:gray25'>N = %s</span>",

      # no, pct not empty -> add percentages
      sprintf("<span style='font-weight:bold; font-family:Roboto Condensed'>%s</span><br><span style='color:gray25'>N = %s (%s%%)</span>",
                        node,
                        scales::comma(n),

             next_x = next_x,

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
5.2 Preregistered analyses
As preregistered, the two startups were analyzed separately, based on the retained deck viewers. Two-factor ANOVAs (Type III sums of squares) related opening duration and slide coverage to visual fluency, substantive quality, and their interaction, and a logistic regression related positive reactions to the same predictors. Both factors were effect coded (low = −1, high = +1). With this coding, the difference between the high and the low level of a factor, averaged over the two levels of the other factor, is two times its coefficient. The interaction contrast, the fluency effect under high quality minus the fluency effect under low quality, is four times the interaction coefficient. We report these contrasts in seconds for opening duration and in percentage points for slide coverage. For positive reactions, the contrasts are the differences between the model-based probabilities of a positive reaction (predicted probabilities with equal weights over the levels of the other factor), in percentage points, with delta-method confidence intervals and z tests. The preregistered Wald tests of the logistic regression refer to the log-odds scale. They agree with the percentage-point tests on the main effects and differ on the interaction, so we report both for the interaction. The preregistration predicted that both factors would increase all three outcomes (for visual fluency, Hypothesis 1) and specified the fluency × quality interaction without a directional prediction. All tests are two-sided (α = .05). To describe the size of the effects, we also computed model-based means at the two levels of each factor, with equal weights over the levels of the other factor and averaged on the response scale (for positive reactions, predicted probabilities), and the percentage increase from the low to the high level. Table 2, Panel A reports the descriptive statistics per condition, Panel B the contrasts and their tests, and Figure 1 shows the fluency and quality effects.
Results. Both visual fluency and substantive quality increased the time investors kept the decks open. High-fluency decks stayed open 42.37 seconds longer than low-fluency decks for the software startup (95% CI [34.69, 50.06]) and 28.65 seconds longer for the healthcare startup (95% CI [22.19, 35.12], both p < .001), increases of 34.8% and 34.0% over the model-based means of the low-fluency decks. Higher substantive quality increased opening duration by 44.50 and 27.74 seconds (both p < .001). Visual fluency also increased slide coverage, by 5.92 percentage points for the software startup (95% CI [4.23, 7.60]) and by 9.28 percentage points for the healthcare startup (95% CI [7.23, 11.33], both p < .001). Higher substantive quality increased slide coverage by 5.59 and 9.64 percentage points (both p < .001). Visual fluency also increased positive reactions. The model-based probability of a positive reaction rose from 5.26% for the low-fluency software decks to 9.75% for the high-fluency versions, and from 6.74% to 13.03% for the healthcare startup, increases of 4.49 percentage points (95% CI [2.95, 6.03]) and 6.29 percentage points (95% CI [3.93, 8.66], both p < .001) or relative increases of 85.3% and 93.4%. Higher substantive quality increased the probability of a positive reaction by 4.51 and 6.64 percentage points, or by 85.9% and 101.1% (both p < .001). The fluency results support Hypothesis 1. For the software startup, the fluency × quality interactions showed a stronger fluency effect for the low-quality deck on opening duration (p = .015), slide coverage (p = .042), and, on the log-odds scale of the preregistered logistic regression, positive reactions (z = -3.52, p < .001). In percentage points, the fluency effect on positive reactions was also smaller for the high-quality deck, by 2.61 points, but this difference was not significant (95% CI [-5.70, 0.48], p = .098). The corresponding interactions for the healthcare startup were not significant (p = .448, p = .351, and p = .630, log-odds scale p = .219).

bind_rows(Software = s1_sw, Healthcare = s1_hc, .id = "startup") |>

  summarize(N = scales::comma(n()),
            dur_mean = f2(mean(duration)), dur_sd = f2(sd(duration)),
            cov_mean = sprintf('%.3f', mean(completion)), cov_sd = sprintf('%.3f', sd(completion)),

5.3 Covariate models
The preregistered robustness models added investment experience (the number of previous startup investments), investor type (reference: business angel), gender (reference: female), and country (reference: United States) to visual fluency, substantive quality, and their interaction, with the same effect coding. They are linear regressions for opening duration and slide coverage (Table C2 for the software startup, Table C3 for the healthcare startup) and a logistic regression for positive reactions. As a further preregistered robustness check, positive reactions were also modeled with a Tobit specification (Tables C4 and C5).
Results. With the covariates, visual fluency and substantive quality increased all three outcomes in both startups (all p < .001), as they did without covariates. The fluency × quality interactions remained negative and significant for the software startup (opening duration p = .013, slide coverage p = .041, positive reactions p < .001) and not significant for the healthcare startup (p = .450, p = .376, and p = .209). The Tobit models showed the same pattern (fluency and quality both p < .001, interaction software p < .001, healthcare p = .303).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
5.4 Domain comparison
The preregistration planned an exploratory comparison of the two startups if the main results differed between the domains, by adding the interaction with the domain to the analyses (AsPredicted #118675). It did not specify the model. For this comparison, we pooled the two samples and fitted a full-factorial model of visual fluency × substantive quality × startup domain for each outcome (linear regressions for opening duration and slide coverage, a logistic regression for positive reactions), with all three factors effect coded (software = +1, healthcare = −1). In these models, four times the fluency × domain and the quality × domain coefficients are the differences between the startups in the fluency and the quality contrasts of Table 2, Panel B (software minus healthcare), and eight times the three-way coefficient is the difference in the interaction contrasts. For positive reactions, the differences between the startups refer to the percentage-point contrasts of Table 2, Panel B, from the model-based probabilities of the pooled logistic regression, with delta-method confidence intervals and z tests. Table C6 reports all nine comparisons.
Results. The fluency and the quality effects on opening duration were larger for the software startup (p = .019 and p = .004), whereas their effects on slide coverage were larger for the healthcare startup (p = .016 and p = .004). Their effects on positive reactions did not differ significantly between the startups (p = .211 and p = .141). The fluency × quality interactions did not differ significantly between the startups for opening duration, slide coverage, or positive reactions (p = .232, p = .579, and p = .191). The significant interactions of the software startup on opening duration and slide coverage and the nonsignificant interactions of the healthcare startup therefore do not establish a difference between the domains.

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
6.1 Sample
Each study used a 2 (visual fluency: high vs. low) × 2 (substantive quality: high vs. low) between-subjects design. Studies 2A and 2B used the software startup’s pitch deck, Study 2C the healthcare startup’s pitch deck. Participants studied one randomly assigned deck on DocSend and then answered the survey in Qualtrics. Qualtrics recorded 318 responses in Study 2A (296 finished), 331 in Study 2B (298 finished), and 329 in Study 2C (299 finished). The preregistered exclusions removed participants without consent, with incomplete responses, with a reported Prolific ID that differed from the recorded one, with a repeated Prolific ID or IP address, who took more than 30 minutes for the survey, whose cumulative deck-viewing time was below 30 seconds or above 30 minutes, who viewed less than 50% of the slides, or who failed the attention or the comprehension check. A further exclusion, which was not preregistered, removed participants whose condition recorded in Qualtrics differed from the deck condition recorded by DocSend. The final samples comprised 197 participants in Study 2A, 200 in Study 2B, and 193 in Study 2C. Table D1 describes the participants.

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
6.2 Preregistered analyses
Each study preregistered a two-factor ANOVA of investment likelihood with visual fluency, substantive quality, and their interaction (α = .05), which we estimated with Type III sums of squares. Both factors were effect coded (low = −1, high = +1). The contrasts in Table 3 are the differences between the high and the low condition in percentage points, estimated in the same factorial models as two times the effect-coded coefficient, so that they average equally over the two levels of the other factor. The interaction contrast, four times the interaction coefficient, is the fluency contrast under high substantive quality minus the fluency contrast under low substantive quality. All tests and 95% confidence intervals are two-sided. Study 2A preregistered positive effects of visual fluency and substantive quality and a test of the fluency × quality interaction without a directional prediction. Following Study 2A’s fluency result, Studies 2B and 2C preregistered that visual fluency would not increase investment likelihood, together with a positive effect of substantive quality and no significant interaction. Table 3 reports the contrasts, Table D2 the condition counts, means, and standard deviations, and Table D3, Panel A the ANOVAs.
Results. Visual fluency did not significantly affect investment likelihood in any of the three studies (Study 2A: Δ = -3.38 percentage points, 95% CI [-10.95, 4.20], p = .380; Study 2B: Δ = 2.03, 95% CI [-5.67, 9.73], p = .604; Study 2C: Δ = 7.17, 95% CI [-0.55, 14.90], p = .069). Study 2A thus did not support its preregistered positive fluency effect. As preregistered, substantive quality significantly increased investment likelihood in all three studies, by 7.89 percentage points in Study 2A (p = .041), 13.11 in Study 2B (p < .001), and 8.94 in Study 2C (p = .024). None of the fluency × quality interactions was significant (Study 2A p = .571, Study 2B p = .841, Study 2C p = .221).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
6.3 Covariate models
The preregistered robustness regressions added age, gender, years of startup investment experience, and the centrality of visual product aesthetics (CVPA, the mean of the 11 items, each from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) to the two effect-coded factors and their interaction (Table D3, Panel B). Gender was entered with female as the reference category, and the answers “Non-binary” and “Prefer not to say” were combined into the category “Other” (only in Study 2B, 4 participants). The preregistrations specified a robust regression instead if Levene’s test indicated unequal group variances. We therefore tested investment likelihood across the fluency conditions, across the quality conditions, and across the four cells in each study (nine tests).
Results. None of the nine Levene tests was significant (smallest p = .083), so the regressions were estimated with ordinary least squares. The covariates did not change the conclusions of the ANOVAs. The fluency coefficient was not significant in any study (Study 2A p = .240, Study 2B p = .371, Study 2C p = .052), the quality coefficient was significant in all three studies (Study 2A p = .016, Study 2B p = .004, Study 2C p = .013), and the interaction in none. CVPA was positively associated with investment likelihood in all three studies (b = 14.65, 14.33, and 14.04 percentage points per scale point, all p < .001).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
6.4 Manipulation checks
Studies 2B and 2C measured two manipulation checks after investment likelihood (Study 2A had none): processing ease (“The process of studying this pitch deck was …”, from 0 = difficult to 100 = easy, prefaced by “Irrespective of the content” in Study 2C) and perceived venture quality (the venture’s potential to generate a sustainable competitive advantage and positive returns to the stakeholders, irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design, from 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent). In each study, t-tests compared processing ease between the visual fluency conditions and perceived venture quality between the substantive quality conditions (Table D4). The t-tests used Student’s or Welch’s version, depending on Levene’s test for equal variances (α = .05). All differences are high minus low, and all tests are two-sided. With the t-tests, we deviate from the preregistration of Study 2B, in which we erroneously wrote that we would run a two-factor ANOVA for the manipulation checks. We corrected this mistake in the preregistration of Study 2C.
Results. High-fluency decks were easier to process in both studies (Study 2B: Δ = 7.97 points, 95% CI [0.24, 15.71], p = .043; Study 2C: Δ = 8.45 points, 95% CI [0.09, 16.82], p = .048), and high substantive quality increased perceived venture quality in both studies (Study 2B: Δ = 0.40, 95% CI [0.06, 0.73], p = .020; Study 2C: Δ = 0.53, 95% CI [0.23, 0.83], p < .001).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
7.2 Preregistered contrasts
For each participant \(i\) and task \(s\), we computed a fluency contrast and a quality contrast from the allocations. The fluency contrast is
\[
\text{FC}_{is} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{HF}_{is}} a_{id} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{LF}_{is}} a_{id},
\]
where \(a_{id}\) is the participant’s allocation (in units) to deck \(d\), and \(\text{HF}_{is}\) and \(\text{LF}_{is}\) are the two high and the two low fluency decks that the participant saw in this task. Since each of these two sets contains one high and one low quality deck, substantive quality is balanced out of the fluency contrast by construction. The quality contrast \(\text{QC}_{is}\) is defined analogously (the two high minus the two low quality decks). Hypothesis 2 (H5 in the preregistration) predicts a larger fluency contrast in the access task than in the evaluation task and is tested with the task difference of the fluency contrasts,
\[
\text{TD}_{i} = \text{FC}_{i,\text{access}} - \text{FC}_{i,\text{evaluation}},
\]
which is labeled “Task difference” in Table 4, Panel A and Figure 2 (the figure also shows the corresponding difference of the quality contrasts). The four preregistered one-sided tests (the quality contrasts in both tasks, the fluency contrast in the access task, and the task difference of the fluency contrasts) used α = .05 without adjustment. The fluency contrast in the evaluation task was preregistered as a supportive estimate, with its 95% confidence interval and the Bayes factor against zero. Table 4, Panel A reports these contrasts and Panel B the condition means. Figure 2 shows the results visually.
Results. Visual fluency increased allocations in both tasks. High-fluency decks received on average 3.94 more attention tokens than low-fluency decks (95% CI [2.14, 5.73], one-sided p < .001) and 4.40 more units of investment capital (95% CI [2.69, 6.12], BF10 = 1.16 × 104). Higher substantive quality increased allocations by 9.72 attention tokens (95% CI [7.74, 11.71]) and by 11.51 units of investment capital (95% CI [9.43, 13.59], both one-sided p < .001). The predicted larger fluency effect in the access task (Hypothesis 2) was not supported: the task difference of the fluency contrasts was -0.50 (95% CI [-2.81, 1.82], one-sided p = .663). The fluency × quality interactions, which were preregistered without a directional prediction, were not significant in either task (access task p = .537, evaluation task p = .167; see Table E2, Panel A).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
7.3 Secondary analyses
The preregistered secondary analyses comprised a 2 (visual fluency) × 2 (substantive quality) repeated-measures ANOVA for each task and a 2 (task) × 2 (visual fluency) × 2 (substantive quality) repeated-measures ANOVA for both tasks, based on the participants with four valid decks in the respective task (Table E2, Panel A). The task main effect is structurally zero because every participant allocated 100 units in each task, so it has no substantive interpretation. The preregistered covariate model regressed the task difference of the fluency contrasts on centered age, investment experience, and centrality of visual product aesthetics, and on gender (male = +1, female = −1; the 2 participants who chose another option are not included in this analysis). Its intercept is the covariate-adjusted task difference. A preregistered exploratory regression related the task difference to centered fatigue. Table E2, Panel B reports both analyses.
Results. Visual fluency and substantive quality increased allocations in both tasks, without supporting the predicted larger fluency effect in the access task (task × fluency interaction, p = .674). The fluency × quality interaction was not significant in either task or in the combined analysis, and neither was the three-way interaction (p = .647). The covariate-adjusted task difference did not support a larger fluency effect in the access task either (-0.14, 95% CI [-2.64, 2.36], one-sided p = .544), and fatigue showed no significant association with the task difference (b = 0.39, 95% CI [-0.93, 1.72], p = .559).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
8.2 Preregistered contrasts
For each participant \(i\), we computed a fluency contrast from the perceived venture quality ratings,
\[
\text{FC}_{i} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{HF}_{i}} r_{id} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{LF}_{i}} r_{id},
\]
where \(r_{id}\) is the participant’s rating (1–7) of deck \(d\), and \(\text{HF}_{i}\) and \(\text{LF}_{i}\) are the two high and the two low fluency decks that the participant saw. Since each of these two sets contains one high and one low quality deck, substantive quality is balanced out of the fluency contrast by construction. The fluency contrast on the allocations is defined analogously (in units). All preregistered tests use the analyzable sample and α = .05. Hypotheses 3, 4, and 5 are H1, H2, and H3 in the preregistration. Hypothesis 3 predicts a positive fluency contrast on the ratings in the control condition and was tested with a one-sided one-sample t-test. Hypothesis 4 predicts that the fluency contrast remains positive in the disclosure condition. It was tested with a two-sided one-sample t-test, together with the 95% confidence interval, the Bayes factor against the point null of zero (BF10, Cauchy prior, r = 0.707), and an equivalence test against the bounds of −0.225 and +0.225 rating points (two one-sided tests, TOST). Equivalence requires that both one-sided tests are significant, which is the same as the 90% confidence interval lying within both bounds. Hypothesis 5 predicts a smaller fluency contrast in the disclosure plus explanation condition than in the disclosure condition and was tested with a one-sided Welch t-test of the difference between the two conditions (Disclosure − explanation). A further preregistered two-sided Welch t-test compared the control and the disclosure condition (Control − disclosure). The fluency contrast on the allocations was preregistered with a one-sided test in the control condition and a two-sided test in the disclosure condition, and the same contrast in the disclosure plus explanation condition was preregistered as exploratory. Table 5, Panel A reports the results for the ratings and Table 5, Panel B those for the allocations. Panel A also shows the effect of substantive quality on the ratings, the preregistered manipulation check in the control condition (see Manipulation checks).
The preregistration applied the following decision rule to the fluency contrast in the disclosure condition, with the cases checked in this order:

The contrast is significantly negative with the estimate at or beyond −0.225: overcorrection.
The contrast is significantly positive with the estimate at least 0.225: persistence supported.
Equivalence holds and the fluency contrast is significantly larger in the control condition (Control − disclosure): switched off (a significant effect within the bounds is reported as such, in either direction).
The contrast is significantly positive but below 0.225, without equivalence: reduced but present.
Otherwise: indeterminate.

In addition, the preregistration required that disclosure lowered the first belief item relative to the control condition before the result could be interpreted as a test of design’s informational role (see Belief check).
Results. In the control condition, high-fluency decks received higher quality ratings than low-fluency decks (Δ = 0.57, 95% CI [0.31, 0.82], one-sided p < .001), which supports Hypothesis 3. Disclosure lowered how much participants reported that the design told them about venture quality, from 3.99 in the control condition to 2.76 (one-sided p < .001, see Table F2, Panel A), which meets the preregistered prerequisite. Under disclosure, high-fluency decks still received higher quality ratings (Δ = 0.39, 95% CI [0.27, 0.51], two-sided p < .001, BF10 = 4.37 × 107). The estimate exceeded 0.225, and its 90% confidence interval [0.29, 0.49] lay above the upper equivalence bound (TOST p = .997). This is case 2 of the decision rule (persistence supported), which supports Hypothesis 4 for the disclosure condition as a whole. The difference between the control and the disclosure condition was not significant (Control − disclosure = 0.17, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.46], two-sided p = .224), so whether disclosure reduced the effect in part remains open. With the added explanation of processing ease, the fluency contrast was 0.38 (95% CI [0.20, 0.55]), compared with 0.39 under disclosure alone. The difference between the two conditions did not support Hypothesis 5 (Disclosure − explanation = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.23], one-sided p = .439). Its confidence interval includes further reductions of up to 0.23 rating points, so the result does not show that the explanation had no effect. Higher substantive quality increased perceived venture quality in the control condition (Δ = 0.88, 95% CI [0.64, 1.12], p < .001).
High-fluency decks received on average 6.16 more units of investment capital than low-fluency decks in the control condition (95% CI [2.39, 9.93], one-sided p < .001). In the disclosure condition, the contrast was 1.73 units (95% CI [-0.13, 3.59], two-sided p = .069). Since the preregistration considered the allocations too noisy for an equivalence test at this sample size, this nonsignificant result does not show that the effect was absent. In the disclosure plus explanation condition, the preregistered exploratory estimate was 2.39 units (95% CI [-0.35, 5.13], two-sided p = .087).

8.3 Belief check
After the allocation, participants rated how much the visual design of the decks had told them about the ventures’ quality (item 1) and about their founders’ competence (item 2), from 1 (nothing at all) to 7 (a great deal). The preregistered belief check was a one-sided Welch t-test of item 1 (disclosure lower than control). Item 2 was compared between the same two conditions with a two-sided Welch t-test, which was not preregistered. Both tests use the analyzable sample. Table F2, Panel A shows the means per condition and the two tests.
Results. Disclosure lowered item 1 from 3.99 in the control condition to 2.76 (Disclosure − control = -1.23, 95% CI [-1.60, -0.86], one-sided p < .001), which meets the preregistered prerequisite. The mean in the disclosure plus explanation condition was 2.74. The answers still varied within the disclosure condition (SD = 1.97). Item 2 decreased similarly (Disclosure − control = -1.20, 95% CI [-1.58, -0.81], two-sided p < .001).

title: Reproducibility Report
text:
8.5 Factual recovery
After each deck, participants answered one four-option question about a fact in its substantive content. The preregistered analysis was a mixed logistic regression in the disclosure condition that predicts a correct answer from visual fluency and substantive quality (both effect-coded), with random intercepts for participants and startups, and in which only the fluency effect is interpreted. With effect coding, the odds ratio of a correct answer after high- vs. low-fluency decks is exp(2 × coefficient). We used the bobyqa optimizer, because the model does not converge with the default optimizer. The model includes the answers to all valid decks (Table F2, Panel C).
Results. In the disclosure condition, participants answered 71.11% of the questions correctly after high-fluency decks and 70.07% after low-fluency decks. The fluency effect was not significant (odds ratio = 1.07, 95% CI [0.86, 1.33], p = .537), so there is no evidence that fluent design helped participants recover the facts.

The preregistered manipulation checks used the control condition only: mixed-effects models of processing ease (0–100) by visual fluency and of perceived venture quality (1–7) by substantive quality, with random intercepts for participants and startups and two-sided tests. title: Reproducibility Report
text:
8.7 Preregistered exploratory analyses
The preregistration listed the following analyses as exploratory, without directional predictions, so all tests are two-sided. All models are mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants and startups, the factors are effect-coded, and invalid decks are not included.

8.7.1 Fluency × quality interactions
For the ratings and for the allocations, we estimated the fluency × quality interaction in each condition, and the fluency × quality × condition interaction for the two disclosure conditions, which tests whether the added explanation changes the fluency × quality interaction (Table F3, Panel A). With effect coding, four times the coefficient of a two-way interaction is the fluency effect at high quality minus the fluency effect at low quality, and eight times the coefficient of the three-way interaction is this difference in the disclosure condition minus that in the disclosure plus explanation condition. The models for the allocations have a singular fit, because the allocations of every participant add up to 100 and the participant intercepts thus have a variance of zero. The fixed effects are not affected by this.
Results. None of the fluency × quality interactions was significant, neither for the ratings (smallest p = .110) nor for the allocations (smallest p = .144), and the interaction did not differ between the two disclosure conditions (ratings p = .347, allocations p = .369). Thus, there is no evidence that visual fluency changed how strongly the ratings or the allocations responded to substantive quality, with or without the explanation.

8.7.3 Order and position effects
First, we tested whether the rating of a deck depends on the position in which the deck was viewed (1–4) or on the position of its rating page (1–4), controlling for visual fluency and substantive quality (all conditions, positions as factors, type III tests with Satterthwaite’s degrees of freedom; Table F3, Panel C). title: Reproducibility Report
text:
8.8 Sensitivity analyses
The preregistration specified two separate sensitivity analyses of Hypothesis 4, which repeat the analysis of the disclosure condition (a) without the participants who needed all three instruction attempts, including those who failed all three, and (b) without the participants who answered “Maybe a little” or “Yes” to the question whether they had formed a guess about what we were testing that might have changed their answers. Each restriction was applied to all conditions, so that the comparison with the control condition in the decision rule uses the same restricted sample. Restriction (a) removed 42 participants from the analyzable sample (control 0, disclosure 32, disclosure plus explanation 10), and restriction (b) removed 211 (control 29, disclosure 122, disclosure plus explanation 60). Table F3, Panel E shows the results next to those of the analyzable sample.
Results. Neither restriction changed the conclusion. The fluency contrast in the disclosure condition was 0.40 (95% CI [0.28, 0.52], BF10 = 2.84 × 107) without the participants who needed three attempts and 0.41 (95% CI [0.27, 0.54], BF10 = 1.59 × 106) without those who reported a possible hypothesis guess. In both analyses, the 90% confidence interval lay above the upper equivalence bound. The decision rule yielded case 2 in restriction (a) and case 2 in restriction (b).

title: Reproducibility Report
section: 8.9 Belief responses in the disclosure condition
text:
8.9 Belief responses in the disclosure condition
Note: The following analysis was not preregistered. In the disclosure condition (analyzable sample), we split the participants by their answer to belief item 1 into those who answered “nothing at all” (1) and those who gave a higher answer, and we computed the fluency contrasts on the ratings and on the allocations in each group, with two-sided 95% confidence intervals. The beliefs were measured after the decks and the allocation, so these groups are post-treatment groups and do not identify the causal effect of accepting the disclosure or a psychological mechanism.
Results. In the disclosure condition, 233 of 494 participants (47.2%) answered “nothing at all”. Among them, high-fluency decks received quality ratings that were 0.18 points higher (95% CI [0.01, 0.35]) and 0.13 more units of investment capital (95% CI [-2.81, 3.08]). Among the other 261 participants of this condition, the fluency contrasts were 0.58 rating points (95% CI [0.42, 0.74]) and 3.15 units (95% CI [0.80, 5.50]).

title: Study 3: Attention and Investment Allocation
text:
For eight fictitious startups (Servora, Curato, Ironhall, Foliant, Pulsegrid, Paperloom, Sentyl, and Axonmesh), we ran an online experiment in which the same participants made two consecutive decisions about the startups’ pitch decks. In the access task, they distributed 100 attention tokens across four pitch decks according to how much each deck merits further study in a screening process. In the evaluation task, they distributed 100 units of investment capital across four other pitch decks.
To make these allocations consequential, the experiment was incentive-compatible. For each task, one pitch deck was drawn with a probability proportional to the participant’s allocation, and the participant received a bonus of up to £1.00 that was proportional to the substantive quality of this startup (its q-score, as rated by an independent panel of seven large language models, cf. the LLM Ratings Reproducibility Report). Since the high and the low fluency version of a pitch deck had the same q-score, the bonus rewarded substantive quality only. A comprehension question before the first task checked that participants understood this. The q-scores and the individual ratings of the language models are available in the online repository.
In the access task, participants could study each pitch deck for at most 150 seconds: a countdown showed the remaining time, and the next pitch deck appeared automatically once the time had run out (participants could also move on earlier). In the evaluation task, there was no time limit. Within each task, the four pitch decks crossed visual fluency (low vs. high) with substantive quality (low vs. high), resulting in a 2 (task) x 2 (visual fluency) x 2 (substantive quality) within-subjects design. For each startup, there were four versions of the pitch deck (14 slides each), and each participant saw every startup only once. Eight rotation patterns counterbalanced which startups appeared in which task and in which version, and the order of the pitch decks within each task was randomized. At the end of the experiment, participants rated each pitch deck again with respect to how easy it had been to study (processing ease) and the startup’s potential irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design (perceived venture quality). Figure 1 summarizes the procedure.
We ran the experiment on Qualtrics, where the pitch decks were displayed as slide images in a click-through viewer, and recruited the participants via Prolific. For details, see the corresponding AsPredicted preregistration listed in Table 1.

        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - stringr
# - forcats
# - weights
# - afex
# - BayesFactor
# - lme4
# - lmerTest
# - broom
# - performance
# - scales
# - hrbrthemes

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)


# Custom functions
#
# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# position of each block in a Qualtrics "Display Order" string
# -Note: the input are the *_DO columns, so the string might look like
#        "Stage1DeckSlot4|Stage1DeckSlot2|Stage1DeckSlot1|Stage1DeckSlot3"
display_position <- function(x, labels) {
  parts <- stringr::str_split(x, stringr::fixed("|"))
  out <- vapply(
    parts,
    function(p) {
      if (length(p) != length(labels) | anyNA(p) | anyDuplicated(p) > 0) {
        return(rep(NA, length(labels)))
      }
      match(labels, p)
    },
    integer(length(labels))
  )
  out <- as.data.frame(t(out))
  names(out) <- labels
  out
}
#
# total time spent viewing a deck (in seconds)
# -Note: the raw string holds the 14 per-slide viewing times in deciseconds
#        (i.e., tenths of a second), separated by "|"
viewtime_sec <- function(x){
  vapply(stringr::str_split(x, stringr::fixed("|")),
         function(p) sum(as.numeric(p)) / 10, numeric(1))
}
#
# number of slides viewed (i.e., the leading number of the coverage string,
# e.g., "7/14" -> 7)
slides_seen <- function(x){
  as.numeric(stringr::str_extract(x, "^\\d+"))
}
#
# all 14 slide images of a deck loaded without failure (i.e., "14/14;fail=0")
images_ok <- function(x){
  stringr::str_extract(x, "^\\d+") %in% "14" &
    stringr::str_extract(x, "(?<=fail=)\\d+") %in% "0"
}
#
# extract the results of a one-sample t-test of a participant-level contrast
# against zero and Cohen's d_z and put the results together as a table
# -Note: NAs (i.e., participants with at least one invalid deck in the
#        respective task) are removed before the test. The 95% confidence
#        interval is always two-sided.
contrast_tbl <- function(x, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  # perform t-test
  tres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = alternative)
  # perform two-sided t-test to get the (two-sided) 95% confidence interval
  cres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3))
  # construct return df
  df <- data.frame(N = length(x), Mean = NA, SD = NA, CI = NA, test_statistic = NA, p = NA, d = NA)
  # fill values
  df$Mean <- weights::rd(mean(x), 2)
  df$SD <- weights::rd(sd(x), 3)
  df$CI <- paste0("[", weights::rd(cres$conf.int[1], 2), ", ", weights::rd(cres$conf.int[2], 2), "]")
  df$test_statistic <- paste0("t(", tres$parameter, ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic))
  df$p <- pval
  df$d <- weights::rd(mean(x) / sd(x), 2)
  return(df)
}
#
# format a Bayes factor (values above 1,000 in scientific notation,
# e.g., 1.16 × 10^4)
bf_fmt <- function(bf){
  ifelse(bf > 1000,
         paste0(sprintf('%.2f', bf / 10^floor(log10(bf))), " × 10<sup>", floor(log10(bf)), "</sup>"),
         sprintf('%.2f', bf))
}
#
# verbal interpretation of a Bayes factor BF10 (classification of Lee &
# Wagenmakers, 2013, adapted from Jeffreys, 1961) and a table note that
# explains it
bf_label <- function(bf){
  dplyr::case_when(bf > 100 ~ "extreme evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 30 ~ "very strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 10 ~ "strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 3 ~ "moderate evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 1 ~ "anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf == 1 ~ "no evidence for either hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/3 ~ "anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/10 ~ "moderate evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/30 ~ "strong evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/100 ~ "very strong evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   TRUE ~ "extreme evidence for the null hypothesis")
}
bf_note <- function(bf, alternative){
  paste0("BF<sub>10</sub> = ", bf_fmt(bf), " indicates ", bf_label(bf),
         " (classification of Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013). That is, the data are ",
         ifelse(bf >= 1, scales::comma(signif(bf, 3)), scales::comma(signif(1 / bf, 3))),
         " times more likely under ", ifelse(bf >= 1, paste0("the alternative hypothesis (", alternative, ")"),
                                             "the null hypothesis (no effect)"),
         " than under ", ifelse(bf >= 1, "the null hypothesis (no effect).",
                                paste0("the alternative hypothesis (", alternative, ").")))
}
#
# extract repeated-measures ANOVA results (from `afex::aov_ez`) including
# partial eta squared and put the results together as a table
# -Note: all within-subjects factors have only two levels, thus no sphericity
#        correction is needed
anova_rm_tbl <- function(model, ...){
  # get ANOVA table
  d <- anova(model, es = "pes", correction = "none")
  # extract key parameters
  effect <- rownames(d)
  # sum of squares of the effect (as in the other reports), i.e., F times the
  # mean square of the error term (which `afex` reports as MSE) times the
  # degrees of freedom of the effect
  SS <- round(d$F * d$MSE * d$`num Df`, 2)
  df <- d$`num Df`
  df_res <- d$`den Df`
  statistic <- round(d$F, 2)
  pval <- ifelse(d$`Pr(>F)` < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$`Pr(>F)`, 3))
  eta <- ifelse(d$pes < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$pes, 3))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(effect, SS, df, df_res, statistic, pval, eta))
}
#
# summarize a manipulation check: observed number of ratings, mean, and SD per
# condition (high, low) and the test of the manipulated factor in a
# mixed-effects model (from `lmerTest::lmer`, effect coding, random intercepts
# for participants and startups) and put the results together as a table
# -Note: Cohen's d is the model-based difference between the high and the low
#        condition (i.e., two times the coefficient) divided by the square root
#        of the sum of all variance components (Westfall et al., 2014).
#        p-values are based on Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom.
mc_tbl <- function(model, effect, y, group, outcome){
  # observed values per condition
  n <- c(sum(group == "high"), sum(group == "low"))
  m <- c(mean(y[group == "high"]), mean(y[group == "low"]))
  sdv <- c(sd(y[group == "high"]), sd(y[group == "low"]))
  # test of the manipulated factor
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[effect, ]
  pval <- ifelse(fe["Pr(>|t|)"] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(fe["Pr(>|t|)"], 3))
  # standardized effect size
  vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(model))
  d_es <- 2 * fe["Estimate"] / sqrt(sum(vc$vcov))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(DV = c(outcome, ""), condition = c("high", "low"),
                    N = scales::comma(n), Mean = weights::rd(m, 2), SD = weights::rd(sdv, 3),
                    test_statistic = c(paste0("t(", scales::comma(unname(fe["df"]), accuracy = .1), ") = ",
                                              sprintf('%.2f', fe["t value"])), ""),
                    p = c(unname(pval), ""), d = c(weights::rd(unname(d_es), 2), ""),
                    row.names = NULL))
}
# extract GLM results and put the results together as a table
glm_tbl <- function(model, coef_digits = 2, coef_bold = TRUE, p_threshold = 0.05, ...){
  # extract model parameters
  if("tobit" %in% class(model)){ # tobit model -> broom::tidy does not work
    res <- parameters::model_parameters(model)
    res <- res[c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "z", "p")]
    names(res) <- c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")
    # res[] <- lapply(res, function(x) { attributes(x) <- NULL; x })
  } else {
    res <- broom::tidy(model)
  }
  pvals <- res$p.value
  res$estimate <- sprintf(paste0("%.", coef_digits, "f"), res$estimate)
  res$std.error <- sprintf("%.3f", res$std.error)
  res$statistic <- sprintf("%.2f", res$statistic)
  # format p value
  res$p.value <- ifelse(res$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p.value, 3))
  # make estimates bold if below critical p value
  if(coef_bold){
    res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
  }
  # bind R2 and Adj. R2 to model parameters
  r2 <- performance::r2(model) # extract R2
  end <- nrow(res) + seq_len(length(r2))
  res[end,"term"] <- names(r2)
  res[end,"estimate"] <- weights::rd(unlist(r2), digits = 3)
  # return result
  return(res)
}

title: Study 3: Attention and Investment Allocation
text:
4.1 Main analyses
As preregistered, we computed for each participant and task a fluency contrast and a quality contrast from the allocation shares (in percentage points). The fluency contrast of participant \(i\) in task \(s\) is
\[
\text{FC}_{is} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{HF}_{is}} a_{id} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{LF}_{is}} a_{id},
\]
where \(a_{id}\) is the participant’s allocation share (in %) to deck \(d\), and \(\text{HF}_{is}\) and \(\text{LF}_{is}\) are the two high and the two low fluency decks that the participant saw in this task. Since each of these two sets contains one high and one low quality deck, substantive quality is balanced out of the fluency contrast by construction. The quality contrast \(\text{QC}_{is}\) is defined analogously (the two high minus the two low quality decks, each set containing one high and one low fluency deck). For example, a fluency contrast of 10 means that the two high fluency decks received, on average, 10 percentage points more of the participant’s allocation than the two low fluency decks. The focal task difference is the difference between the fluency contrasts of the two tasks, \(\text{FC}_{i,\text{access}} - \text{FC}_{i,\text{evaluation}}\).
Table 5 (a) shows the results of the preregistered one-sided one-sample t-tests of the contrasts against zero (predicted direction: positive) for the quality and the fluency contrast in the access task, the quality contrast in the evaluation task, and the task difference of the fluency contrasts (the focal test). No alpha adjustment was applied across these four tests. For the fluency contrast in the evaluation task, which was not preregistered as a confirmatory test, Table 5 (b) reports the point estimate, the 95% confidence interval, the two-sided test, and the Bayes factor (BF10; default Cauchy prior with r = 0.707, two-sided, point null at zero). All confidence intervals are two-sided, also for the one-sided tests. In the preregistration, these five contrasts correspond to the hypotheses H1 (quality contrast, access task), H2 (fluency contrast, access task), H3 (quality contrast, evaluation task), H4 (fluency contrast, evaluation task), and H5 (task difference of the fluency contrasts, Hypothesis 2 in the paper).

We also preregistered repeated-measures ANOVAs as secondary tests: a 2 (visual fluency) x 2 (substantive quality) ANOVA for each task and a 2 (task) x 2 (visual fluency) x 2 (substantive quality) ANOVA for both tasks together. Table 6 shows the results of these ANOVAs, which are based on the same participants as the corresponding contrasts (i.e., participants with four valid decks in the respective task). The ANOVAs use type III sums of squares. The table reports the sum of squares of each effect (SS) and partial eta squared as effect size (ηp2). The F-tests of the ANOVAs correspond to two-sided tests: the main effects of fluency and quality and the task × fluency interaction are equivalent to the two-sided t-tests of the corresponding contrasts (i.e., F = t2). For example, the task × fluency interaction has a two-sided p-value of .674, whereas the task difference in Table 5 (a) has a one-sided p-value of .663. For estimates in the predicted direction, it equals half the two-sided p-value.

title: Study 3: Attention and Investment Allocation
text:
4.2 Manipulation checks
In this section, we report the results of the manipulation checks for visual fluency and substantive quality. At the end of the experiment, participants rated each of the eight decks with respect to how easy it had been to study the pitch deck (processing ease, from 0 = difficult to 100 = easy) and with respect to the startup’s potential irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design (perceived venture quality, from 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent). Since the observation-level exclusions only apply to the allocations, the manipulation checks use all decks of all participants.
As preregistered, we estimated two mixed-effects models, one that predicts processing ease by visual fluency and one that predicts perceived venture quality by substantive quality, both with random intercepts for participants and startups and with effect coding (i.e., low as -1 and high as +1). For processing ease and perceived venture quality, Table 7 (a) and Table 7 (b) show the observed (i.e., not model-based) mean ratings per condition, together with the test of the respective factor in the mixed-effects model (Satterthwaite’s degrees of freedom) and a standardized effect size.

title: Study 3: Attention and Investment Allocation
text:
4.3 Robustness check
As a preregistered robustness check, we estimated a linear regression model in which we predicted the task difference by age, gender, investment experience, and the centrality of visual product aesthetics (CVPA). For the intercept to be the covariate-adjusted mean contrast, we centered all continuous covariates and used effect coding for gender (i.e., we coded Female as -1 and Male as +1, so that participants in the gender category Other were not included in this model).1 As preregistered, the intercept (i.e., the covariate-adjusted task difference) was evaluated one-sided as the focal robustness test. Table 8 shows the results of this regression. For the intercept, the table reports both the two-sided and the one-sided p-value. The one-sided p-value is half the two-sided p-value if the estimate has the predicted (i.e., positive) sign, and one minus half the two-sided p-value otherwise.


Code
# for the regressions, we keep only participants with a valid stage x fluency
# contrast, so that the covariates are centered within the analysis sample
d_rob <- d |> filter(!is.na(stage_x_fluency_contrast))

# center the continuous covariates
d_rob$age_c <- scale(d_rob$age, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
d_rob$invest_experience_c <- scale(d_rob$invest_experience, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
d_rob$CVPA_c <- scale(d_rob$CVPA, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)
# effect coding for gender (Male = 1, Female = -1, Other = NA)
d_rob$gender_e <- NA
d_rob$gender_e[d_rob$gender == "Male"] <- 1
d_rob$gender_e[d_rob$gender == "Female"] <- -1

# run regression
m_rob <- lm(stage_x_fluency_contrast ~ age_c + gender_e + invest_experience_c + CVPA_c, d_rob)
glm_tbl(m_rob, coef_bold = FALSE) -> lm_rob

# one-sided p-value of the intercept (alternative: intercept > 0)
# --Note: `summary` reports two-sided p-values, thus we compute the one-sided
#         p-value from the t-value of the intercept
p_intercept <- pt(coef(summary(m_rob))["(Intercept)", "t value"],
                  df = m_rob$df.residual, lower.tail = FALSE)
lm_rob$p_one_sided <- NA
lm_rob$p_one_sided[1] <- weights::rd(p_intercept, 3)

lm_rob |>
  mutate(term = c("Intercept", "Age (centered)", "Gender (male = +1, female = -1)",
                  "Investment experience (centered)", "CVPA (centered)",
                  "R<sup>2</sup>", "R<sup>2</sup><sub>adj.</sub>")) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("", "Coeff.", "SE", "t", "p (two-sided)", "p (one-sided)"),
      escape = FALSE, align = "lccccc") |>
