title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
For the same eight fictitious startups as in Study 3 (Servora, Curato, Ironhall, Foliant, Pulsegrid, Paperloom, Sentyl, and Axonmesh), we ran an online experiment in which we varied what participants were told about the visual design of the pitch decks. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three instruction conditions (control, disclosure, and disclosure plus explanation) in a 1:5:2 ratio. Before reviewing the pitch decks, they read one of the following messages:

Control: “You will review four startup pitch decks and at the end distribute 100 units of investment capital across them. Please review each pitch deck and judge the venture from the venture information presented.”
Disclosure: “You will review four startup pitch decks and at the end distribute 100 units of investment capital across them. The visual design of the decks was created by a design agency for this study. The founders did not create or choose it. The design tells you nothing about the ventures or their founders. Please review each pitch deck and judge each venture from the venture information presented.”
Disclosure plus explanation: the disclosure message with two additional sentences before its final sentence: “You will review four startup pitch decks and at the end distribute 100 units of investment capital across them. The visual design of the decks was created by a design agency for this study. The founders did not create or choose it. The design tells you nothing about the ventures or their founders. Visual design can make the same information feel easier or harder to process. That feeling is not evidence about the venture. Please review each pitch deck and judge each venture from the venture information presented.”

After the message, participants answered two comprehension questions about it (in the control condition, about the logistics of the study). A wrong answer led to a notice and a repeated presentation of the message (up to three attempts). After the second pitch deck, participants saw a short reminder of their message.
The experiment was incentive-compatible: at the end, participants distributed 100 units of investment capital across the four startups they had reviewed, one startup was drawn with a probability proportional to its allocation, and the participant received a bonus of up to £1.00 that was proportional to the substantive quality of this startup (its q-score, as rated by an independent panel of seven large language models, cf. the LLM Ratings Reproducibility Report). Since the high and the low fluency version of a pitch deck had the same q-score, the bonus rewarded substantive quality only. The q-scores and the individual ratings of the language models are available in the online repository. Participants who answered the comprehension question about the bonus incorrectly twice were screened out during the study and compensated for their time.
Each participant reviewed four of the eight startups, one pitch deck for each combination of visual fluency (low vs. high) and substantive quality (low vs. high), resulting in a 3 (instruction condition; between-subjects) x 2 (visual fluency; within-subjects) x 2 (substantive quality; within-subjects) design. Sixteen rotation patterns counterbalanced which startups a participant saw and in which version. Before and after the reminder, participants saw one high and one low fluency pitch deck each, in random order. There was no time limit. After each pitch deck, participants answered a factual question about the startup (factual recovery). After the investment allocation, they answered questions about the study’s purpose and indicated how much the visual design had told them about the startups’ quality and the founders’ competence (beliefs). Finally, participants saw each pitch deck again and rated it with respect to how easy it had been to study (processing ease; called felt ease in the preregistration) and the startup’s potential irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design (perceived venture quality, the main dependent variable). Figure 1 summarizes the procedure.
We ran the experiment on Qualtrics, where the pitch decks were displayed as slide images in a click-through viewer, and recruited the participants via Prolific. For details, see the corresponding AsPredicted preregistration listed in Table 1.

options(knitr.kable.NA = '')

# setup
library(here)

options(knitr.kable.NA = '',
        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - stringr
# - forcats
# - weights
# - BayesFactor
# - lme4
# - lmerTest
# - scales
# - hrbrthemes

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)

# preregistered equivalence bound for H2 (in rating points)
eq_bound <- 0.225


# Custom functions
#
# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# position of each block in a Qualtrics "Display Order" string
# -Note: the input are the *_DO columns, so the string might look like
#        "FeltEaseSlot3|FeltEaseSlot1|FeltEaseSlot4|FeltEaseSlot2"
display_position <- function(x, labels) {
  parts <- stringr::str_split(x, stringr::fixed("|"))
  out <- vapply(
    parts,
    function(p) {
      if (length(p) != length(labels) | anyNA(p) | anyDuplicated(p) > 0) {
        return(rep(NA, length(labels)))
      }
      match(labels, p)
    },
    integer(length(labels))
  )
  out <- as.data.frame(t(out))
  names(out) <- labels
  out
}
#
# total time spent viewing a deck (in seconds)
# -Note: the raw string holds the 14 per-slide viewing times in deciseconds
#        (i.e., tenths of a second), separated by "|"
viewtime_sec <- function(x){
  vapply(stringr::str_split(x, stringr::fixed("|")),
         function(p) sum(as.numeric(p)) / 10, numeric(1))
}
#
# number of slides viewed (i.e., the leading number of the coverage string,
# e.g., "7/14" -> 7)
slides_seen <- function(x){
  as.numeric(stringr::str_extract(x, "^\\d+"))
}
#
# all 14 slide images of a deck loaded without failure (i.e., "14/14;fail=0")
images_ok <- function(x){
  stringr::str_extract(x, "^\\d+") %in% as.character(14) &
    stringr::str_extract(x, "(?<=fail=)\\d+") %in% "0"
}
#
# extract the results of a one-sample t-test of a participant-level contrast
# against zero and Cohen's d_z and put the results together as a table
# -Note: NAs (i.e., participants with at least one invalid deck) are removed
#        before the test. The 95% confidence interval is always two-sided.
contrast_tbl <- function(x, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  # perform t-test
  tres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = alternative)
  # perform two-sided t-test to get the (two-sided) 95% confidence interval
  cres <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3))
  # construct return df
  df <- data.frame(N = length(x), Mean = NA, SD = NA, CI = NA, test_statistic = NA, p = NA, d = NA)
  # fill values
  df$Mean <- weights::rd(mean(x), 2)
  df$SD <- weights::rd(sd(x), 3)
  df$CI <- paste0("[", weights::rd(cres$conf.int[1], 2), ", ", weights::rd(cres$conf.int[2], 2), "]")
  df$test_statistic <- paste0("t(", tres$parameter, ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic))
  df$p <- pval
  df$d <- weights::rd(mean(x) / sd(x), 2)
  return(df)
}
#
# format a Bayes factor (values above 1,000 in scientific notation,
# e.g., 4.37 × 10^7)
bf_fmt <- function(bf){
  ifelse(bf > 1000,
         paste0(sprintf('%.2f', bf / 10^floor(log10(bf))), " × 10<sup>", floor(log10(bf)), "</sup>"),
         sprintf('%.2f', bf))
}
#
# verbal interpretation of a Bayes factor BF10 (classification of Lee &
# Wagenmakers, 2013, adapted from Jeffreys, 1961) and a table note that
# explains it
bf_label <- function(bf){
  dplyr::case_when(bf > 100 ~ "extreme evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 30 ~ "very strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 10 ~ "strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 3 ~ "moderate evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf > 1 ~ "anecdotal evidence for the alternative hypothesis",
                   bf == 1 ~ "no evidence for either hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/3 ~ "anecdotal evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/10 ~ "moderate evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/30 ~ "strong evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   bf > 1/100 ~ "very strong evidence for the null hypothesis",
                   TRUE ~ "extreme evidence for the null hypothesis")
}
bf_note <- function(bf, alternative){
  paste0("BF<sub>10</sub> = ", bf_fmt(bf), " indicates ", bf_label(bf),
         " (classification of Lee & Wagenmakers, 2013). That is, the data are ",
         ifelse(bf >= 1, scales::comma(signif(bf, 3)), scales::comma(signif(1 / bf, 3))),
         " times more likely under ", ifelse(bf >= 1, paste0("the alternative hypothesis (", alternative, ")"),
                                             "the null hypothesis (no effect)"),
         " than under ", ifelse(bf >= 1, "the null hypothesis (no effect).",
                                paste0("the alternative hypothesis (", alternative, ").")))
}
#
# extract the results of a Welch two-sample t-test and Cohen's d and put the
# results together as a table
# -Note: Cohen's d uses the average of the two variances as the standardizer
#        (since the Welch test does not assume equal variances)
welch_tbl <- function(x, y, alternative = "two.sided", ...){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  y <- y[!is.na(y)]
  # perform Welch t-test
  tres <- t.test(x, y, alternative = alternative, var.equal = FALSE)
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(tres$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(tres$p.value, 3))
  # construct return df
  df <- data.frame(N_1 = length(x), N_2 = length(y), Mean_1 = NA, Mean_2 = NA,
                   test_statistic = NA, p = NA, d = NA)
  # fill values
  df$Mean_1 <- weights::rd(mean(x), 2)
  df$Mean_2 <- weights::rd(mean(y), 2)
  df$test_statistic <- paste0("t(", weights::rd(tres$parameter, 1), ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', tres$statistic))
  df$p <- pval
  df$d <- weights::rd((mean(x) - mean(y)) / sqrt((var(x) + var(y)) / 2), 2)
  return(df)
}
#
# extract the results of an equivalence test (two one-sided tests, TOST) of a
# participant-level contrast against the bounds -bound and +bound and put the
# results together as a table
# -Note: equivalence is concluded if both one-sided tests are significant at
#        alpha = .05, which is the same as the 90% CI lying inside the bounds
tost_tbl <- function(x, bound = eq_bound, ...){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  # perform the two one-sided tests
  res_lower <- t.test(x, mu = -bound, alternative = "greater")
  res_upper <- t.test(x, mu = bound, alternative = "less")
  # construct p-values
  p_lower <- ifelse(res_lower$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res_lower$p.value, 3))
  p_upper <- ifelse(res_upper$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res_upper$p.value, 3))
  # construct return df
  df <- data.frame(test = c(paste0("Lower bound: mean > -", bound), paste0("Upper bound: mean < +", bound)),
                   test_statistic = c(paste0("t(", res_lower$parameter, ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', res_lower$statistic)),
                                      paste0("t(", res_upper$parameter, ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', res_upper$statistic))),
                   p = c(p_lower, p_upper))
  return(df)
}
#
# preregistered decision rule for H2 (steps applied in the preregistered order)
# -Note: x = fluency contrast in the disclosure condition,
#        x_control = fluency contrast in the control condition
h2_decision <- function(x, x_control, bound = eq_bound){
  # remove missing values
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  x_control <- x_control[!is.na(x_control)]
  # estimate and two-sided test against zero
  est <- mean(x)
  p_zero <- t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided")$p.value
  sig_negative <- p_zero < .05 & est < 0
  sig_positive <- p_zero < .05 & est > 0
  # equivalence test (TOST)
  p_lower <- t.test(x, mu = -bound, alternative = "greater")$p.value
  p_upper <- t.test(x, mu = bound, alternative = "less")$p.value
  equivalence <- p_lower < .05 & p_upper < .05
  # control vs. disclosure (Welch t-test, two-sided): control effect higher?
  p_comparison <- t.test(x_control, x, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value
  control_higher <- p_comparison < .05 & mean(x_control) > est
  # decision rule
  if (sig_negative & est <= -bound) {
    return("(1) significantly negative with the estimate at or beyond the bound: overcorrection")
  }
  if (sig_positive & est >= bound) {
    return("(2) significantly positive with the estimate at least 0.225: persistence supported")
  }
  if (equivalence & control_higher) {
    if (sig_positive) return("(3) switched off (a significantly positive effect remains inside the bound)")
    if (sig_negative) return("(3) switched off (a significantly negative effect remains inside the bound)")
    return("(3) switched off")
  }
  if (sig_positive & est < bound & !equivalence) {
    return("(4) significantly positive below 0.225 without passing equivalence: reduced but present")
  }
  return("(5) indeterminate")
}
#
# step number and outcome of the decision rule for H2, taken from the text that
# `h2_decision` returns (e.g., "(2) significantly positive ...: H2 supported"
# -> step 2, outcome "prediction supported")
h2_step <- function(decision){
  as.integer(stringr::str_extract(decision, "(?<=^\\()\\d"))
}
h2_outcome <- function(decision){
  outcome <- stringr::str_remove(stringr::str_remove(decision, "^\\(\\d\\) "), "^.*: ")
  stringr::str_replace(outcome, "H2 ", "prediction ")
}
#
# summarize a manipulation check: observed number of ratings, mean, and SD per
# condition (high, low) and the test of the manipulated factor in a
# mixed-effects model (from `lmerTest::lmer`, effect coding, random intercepts
# for participants and startups) and put the results together as a table
# -Note: Cohen's d is the model-based difference between the high and the low
#        condition (i.e., two times the coefficient) divided by the square root
#        of the sum of all variance components (Westfall et al., 2014).
#        p-values are based on Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom.
mc_tbl <- function(model, effect, y, group, outcome){
  # observed values per condition
  n <- c(sum(group == "high"), sum(group == "low"))
  m <- c(mean(y[group == "high"]), mean(y[group == "low"]))
  sdv <- c(sd(y[group == "high"]), sd(y[group == "low"]))
  # test of the manipulated factor
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[effect, ]
  pval <- ifelse(fe["Pr(>|t|)"] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(fe["Pr(>|t|)"], 3))
  # standardized effect size
  vc <- as.data.frame(lme4::VarCorr(model))
  d_es <- 2 * fe["Estimate"] / sqrt(sum(vc$vcov))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(DV = c(outcome, ""), condition = c("high", "low"),
                    N = scales::comma(n), Mean = weights::rd(m, 2), SD = weights::rd(sdv, 3),
                    test_statistic = c(paste0("t(", scales::comma(unname(fe["df"]), accuracy = .1), ") = ",
                                              sprintf('%.2f', fe["t value"])), ""),
                    p = c(unname(pval), ""), d = c(weights::rd(unname(d_es), 2), ""),
                    row.names = NULL))
}
#
# summarize factual recovery: observed number of answers and share of correct
# answers per fluency condition (high, low) and the fluency effect in a mixed
# logistic regression (from `lme4::glmer`, effect coding) and put the results
# together as a table
# -Note: with effect coding, the odds ratio (high vs. low) is exp(2 * coefficient)
recovery_tbl <- function(model, y, group){
  # observed values per condition
  n <- c(sum(group == "high"), sum(group == "low"))
  share <- c(mean(y[group == "high"]), mean(y[group == "low"]))
  # fluency effect
  fe <- coef(summary(model))["fluency1", ]
  pval <- ifelse(fe["Pr(>|z|)"] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(fe["Pr(>|z|)"], 3))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(DV = c("Correct answer", ""), condition = c("high", "low"),
                    N = scales::comma(n), share = sprintf('%.1f', 100 * share),
                    test_statistic = c(paste0("z = ", sprintf('%.2f', fe["z value"])), ""),
                    p = c(unname(pval), ""), or = c(sprintf('%.2f', exp(2 * fe["Estimate"])), ""),
                    row.names = NULL))
}
#
# extract a single fixed effect (e.g., an interaction) from a mixed-effects
# model (from `lmerTest::lmer`) and put the results together as a table
# -Note: with effect coding, the coefficient of a two-way interaction is a
#        quarter of the corresponding difference of differences, and the
#        coefficient of a three-way interaction is an eighth of the
#        corresponding difference. Thus, we also report this difference (i.e.,
#        `multiplier` times the coefficient) with its 95% confidence interval
#        (based on Satterthwaite's degrees of freedom), as well as the number of
#        observations and participants.
lmer_coef_tbl <- function(model, effect, multiplier = 4, coef_digits = 2, ...){
  # extract fixed effect
  fe <- coef(summary(model))[effect, ]
  # construct p-value
  pval <- ifelse(fe["Pr(>|t|)"] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(fe["Pr(>|t|)"], 3))
  # implied difference and its 95% confidence interval
  diff <- unname(multiplier * fe["Estimate"])
  diff_se <- unname(multiplier * fe["Std. Error"])
  lower <- diff - qt(.975, unname(fe["df"])) * diff_se
  upper <- diff + qt(.975, unname(fe["df"])) * diff_se
  # construct return df
  fmt <- paste0("%.", coef_digits, "f")
  return(data.frame(estimate = sprintf(fmt, fe["Estimate"]),
                    std.error = sprintf("%.3f", fe["Std. Error"]),
                    difference = sprintf(fmt, diff),
                    ci = paste0("[", sprintf(fmt, lower), ", ", sprintf(fmt, upper), "]"),
                    test_statistic = paste0("t(", scales::comma(unname(fe["df"]), accuracy = .1), ") = ", sprintf('%.2f', fe["t value"])),
                    p = unname(pval),
                    observations = scales::comma(nobs(model)),
                    participants = scales::comma(unname(lme4::ngrps(model)["ID"])),
                    row.names = NULL))
}

title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
4.1 Main analyses
As preregistered, we computed for each participant a fluency contrast on the perceived venture quality ratings (in rating points):
\[
\text{FC}_{i} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{HF}_{i}} r_{id} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{d \in \text{LF}_{i}} r_{id},
\]
where \(r_{id}\) is participant \(i\)’s perceived venture quality rating (1–7) of deck \(d\), and \(\text{HF}_{i}\) and \(\text{LF}_{i}\) are the two high and the two low fluency decks that the participant saw. Since each of these two sets contains one high and one low quality deck, substantive quality is balanced out of the fluency contrast by construction. For completeness, we also computed the analogous quality contrast (the two high minus the two low quality decks) and the same contrasts on the allocated units. For example, a fluency contrast of 0.5 means that the two high fluency decks were rated, on average, half a rating point higher than the two low fluency decks. All confirmatory tests use the analyzable sample (i.e., participants with four valid decks).
The preregistered predictions were that the fluency contrast is positive in the control condition, that it remains positive in the disclosure condition, and that it is smaller in the disclosure plus explanation condition than in the disclosure condition (hypotheses H1, H2, and H3 in the preregistration, Hypotheses 3, 4, and 5 in the paper). Table 6 shows the results of the one-sample t-tests of the fluency contrast against zero. For the control condition (Table 6 (a)), we preregistered a one-sided test (fluency contrast > 0). For the disclosure condition (Table 6 (b)), we preregistered a two-sided test together with the 95% confidence interval and the Bayes factor (BF10; default Cauchy prior with r = 0.707, point null at zero). All confidence intervals are two-sided, also for the one-sided test.



Table 6: Preregistered one-sample t-tests of the fluency contrast (in rating points)

The preregistered decision rule for the disclosure condition was as follows:

The fluency contrast is significantly negative with the estimate at or beyond the bound (-0.225): overcorrection.
The fluency contrast is significantly positive with the estimate at least 0.225: persistence supported.
Equivalence passes and the comparison of the control and the disclosure condition is significant with the fluency contrast being higher in the control condition: switched off (any significant effect remaining inside the bound is reported as such, in either direction).
The fluency contrast is significantly positive but below 0.225 without passing equivalence: reduced but present.
Otherwise: indeterminate.

Applying this decision rule to the results above yields case 2 (persistence supported). Figure 4 shows which case other estimates would have yielded.

title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
4.2 Further preregistered measures
As preregistered, the two further measures (factual recovery and investment allocation) were estimated in the disclosure condition. The same quantities in the other conditions are exploratory (unless noted otherwise). In addition, we preregistered a check of the participants’ beliefs about the informativeness of the design.

4.2.1 Factual recovery
After each deck, participants answered one four-option question about a substantive fact of the startup. We estimated a mixed logistic regression that predicts a correct answer by visual fluency and substantive quality, with random intercepts for participants and startups. As preregistered, only the fluency effect is interpreted, and the preregistered test concerns the disclosure condition. The models for the other two conditions are exploratory. Both factors were effect-coded (i.e., low as -1 and high as +1). With this coding, the difference in log-odds between the high and the low condition is two times the coefficient, and the odds ratio (high vs. low) is thus exp(2 × coefficient). We used the bobyqa optimizer, since the model for the disclosure condition did not converge with the default optimizer. The model for the control condition has a singular fit (i.e., the estimated startup variance is zero). The answers to invalid decks are not included, so that the models are based on all participants with at least one valid deck. Table 8 shows the observed share of correct answers per condition and fluency level, together with the fluency effect in the mixed logistic regressions.

Code
# mixed logistic regressions
#
# convert factors and use effect coding
d_long$fluency <- as.factor(d_long$fluency)
d_long$quality <- as.factor(d_long$quality)
d_long$ID <- as.factor(d_long$ID)
d_long$venture <- as.factor(d_long$venture)
contrasts(d_long$fluency) <- contr.sum # high = 1, low = -1
contrasts(d_long$quality) <- contr.sum # high = 1, low = -1

# answers to valid decks per condition
d_rec_control <- d_long |> filter(condition == "control" & !is.na(recovery_correct))
d_rec_disclosure <- d_long |> filter(condition == "disclosure" & !is.na(recovery_correct))
d_rec_explanation <- d_long |> filter(condition == "disclosure_explanation" & !is.na(recovery_correct))

# control condition (exploratory)
m_rec_control <- lme4::glmer(recovery_correct ~ fluency + quality + (1 | ID) + (1 | venture),
                             data = d_rec_control,
                             family = binomial,
                             control = lme4::glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
# disclosure condition (preregistered)
m_rec_disclosure <- lme4::glmer(recovery_correct ~ fluency + quality + (1 | ID) + (1 | venture),
                                data = d_rec_disclosure,
                                family = binomial,
                                control = lme4::glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
# disclosure plus explanation condition (exploratory)
m_rec_explanation <- lme4::glmer(recovery_correct ~ fluency + quality + (1 | ID) + (1 | venture),
                                 data = d_rec_explanation,
                                 family = binomial,
                                 control = lme4::glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# observed share of correct answers and fluency effect per condition
bind_rows(
  recovery_tbl(m_rec_control, d_rec_control$recovery_correct, d_rec_control$fluency),
  recovery_tbl(m_rec_disclosure, d_rec_disclosure$recovery_correct, d_rec_disclosure$fluency),
  recovery_tbl(m_rec_explanation, d_rec_explanation$recovery_correct, d_rec_explanation$fluency)
) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Outcome", "Fluency Condition", "N", "% Correct", "z-test", "p (two-sided)", "Odds Ratio (High vs. Low)"),

  pack_rows(index = c("Control (Exploratory)" = 2, "Disclosure (Preregistered)" = 2,

4.2.3 Belief check
After the investment allocation, participants indicated how much the visual design of the decks had told them about the startups’ quality (belief item 1) and about their founders’ competence (belief item 2), from 1 = nothing at all to 7 = a great deal. As preregistered, we tested whether disclosure lowered the belief that the design was informative about the startups’ quality, using a Welch t-test on belief item 1 (disclosure vs. control, one-sided, disclosure lower). A signaling interpretation of the result in the disclosure condition requires that disclosure lowered this belief. If the test is not significant, the fluency estimate is reported, but the signaling test is inconclusive. In addition, we compared belief item 2 between the disclosure and the control condition with a Welch t-test (two-sided). This second test was not preregistered and is exploratory. For consistency with the confirmatory tests, we used the analyzable sample. Table 10 (a) shows the mean beliefs per condition, and Table 10 (b) shows the results of the two tests.

title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
4.3 Manipulation checks
In this section, we report the results of the manipulation checks for visual fluency and substantive quality. As preregistered, they use the control condition only. At the end of the experiment, participants rated each deck with respect to how easy it had been to study the pitch deck (processing ease, from 0 = difficult to 100 = easy) and the startup’s potential irrespective of the pitch deck’s visual design (perceived venture quality, from 1 = very poor to 7 = excellent). Since the observation-level exclusions only apply to the deck-level dependent variables, the manipulation checks use all decks of all participants in the control condition.
As preregistered, we estimated two mixed-effects models, one that predicts processing ease by visual fluency and one that predicts perceived venture quality by substantive quality, both with random intercepts for participants and startups and with effect coding (i.e., low as -1 and high as +1). For processing ease and perceived venture quality, Table 11 (a) and Table 11 (b) show the observed (i.e., not model-based) mean ratings per condition, together with the test of the respective factor in the mixed-effects model (Satterthwaite’s degrees of freedom) and a standardized effect size.

Cohen’s d is the model-based difference between the high and the low condition, divided by the square root of the sum of the variance components (Westfall et al., 2014).

title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
4.4 Sensitivity analyses
As preregistered, we re-estimated the analyses of the disclosure condition (a) excluding participants who needed all three attempts to answer the comprehension questions about their instruction message (including those who failed all three attempts), and (b) excluding participants who answered anything other than “No” to the question whether they had formed a guess about what we were testing. In the analyzable sample, 42 participants needed three attempts (control: 0; disclosure: 32; disclosure plus explanation: 10), and 211 participants answered Yes or Maybe a little to the question whether they had formed a guess. The exclusions were applied to all conditions, so that the comparison of the control and the disclosure condition in the decision rule uses the same reduced sample. Table 12 shows the results for the disclosure condition, next to the results for the full analyzable sample.

title: Study 4: Design Disclosure and an Explanation of Processing Ease
text:
4.5 Exploratory analyses
As preregistered, we explored (a) the fluency × quality interaction on the quality ratings and on the allocated units, including whether the added explanation (disclosure plus explanation vs. disclosure) changes it, and (b) order and position effects. Since no directions were preregistered, all tests are two-sided. All models are mixed-effects models with random intercepts for participants and startups, the factors are effect-coded (i.e., low as -1 and high as +1; for the comparison of the two disclosure conditions, disclosure as +1 and disclosure_explanation as -1; for the halves, first as +1 and second as -1; for the sequences, hq_first (high quality decks first) as +1 and lq_first as -1), and invalid decks are not included. With effect coding, the coefficient of a two-way interaction is a quarter of the corresponding difference of differences (e.g., the fluency effect at high quality minus the fluency effect at low quality), and the coefficient of a three-way interaction is an eighth of the corresponding difference (e.g., this difference of differences in the disclosure condition minus that in the disclosure plus explanation condition). The tables therefore also report these differences (i.e., four or eight times the coefficient) with their 95% confidence intervals, as well as the number of observations and participants of each model.
Table 13 shows the fluency × quality interactions per condition and the three-way interaction that tests whether the fluency × quality interaction differs between the two disclosure conditions, for the quality ratings (Table 13 (a)) and for the allocated units (Table 13 (b)). The models for the allocated units have a singular fit: since the allocations of every participant add up to 100, the participant intercepts have a variance of zero. The fixed effects are not affected by this.



Table 13: Exploratory analysis: Fluency × quality interactions (mixed-effects models)

title: Deck Benchmarking
text:
To ensure that our experimental pitch decks appeared realistic and ecologically valid in terms of design and fluency, we benchmarked their visual fluency against 3,510 real pitch decks submitted to a European venture capital (VC) firm specializing in seed-stage investments. Importantly, since these real pitch decks include both successful and unsuccessful funding attempts, this approach mitigates the survivorship bias inherent in publicly available pitch decks, which are typically limited to successful cases and may overrepresent higher visual fluency.
In this report, we first locate all 40 experimental pitch decks of our studies (i.e., the eight decks of Studies 1 and 2 and the 32 decks of Studies 3 and 4) in the benchmark distributions of contrast, simplicity, and symmetry. We then assess how closely the visual fluency of real pitch decks is related to their substantive quality, that is, whether pitch decks with high substantive quality and low visual fluency exist in practice. To this end, two open-weight LLMs rated the substantive quality of each real pitch deck based on its text only. We related these ratings to an image-based fluency score and, in addition, related the fluency score to founder characteristics and venture outcomes that the VC firm recorded.
These analyses were not preregistered.
In what follows, we will give an overview of the results, followed by figures that summarize the results. As this report is dynamically created with R and Quarto, we also report all code. However, for readability, code is hidden by default and only the relevant results are shown.


Code
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')

# setup
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)
library(kableExtra)
options(knitr.kable.NA = '',
        kable_styling_bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed", "responsive"))

# further packages that are loaded on demand are:
# - readr
# - tidyr
# - weights
# - irr
# - broom
# - performance
# - scales
# - hrbrthemes

# set option to disable showing the column types when loading data with `readr`
options("readr.show_col_types" = FALSE)


# Custom functions
#
# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# intraclass correlations of a matrix of ratings (rows = rated decks, columns =
# raters): two-way random effects and absolute agreement for a single rater,
# ICC(2,1), and for the mean of the k raters, ICC(2,k) (Shrout & Fleiss, 1979)
# -Note: rows with missing values are removed
icc_2 <- function(m){
  m <- as.matrix(m)
  m <- m[complete.cases(m), ]
  n <- nrow(m); k <- ncol(m); g <- mean(m)
  # mean squares of the rows (decks), the columns (raters), and the residuals
  ms_rows <- k * sum((rowMeans(m) - g)^2) / (n - 1)
  ms_cols <- n * sum((colMeans(m) - g)^2) / (k - 1)
  ms_error <- sum((m - outer(rowMeans(m), colMeans(m), "+") + g)^2) / ((n - 1) * (k - 1))
  # construct return vector
  return(c(icc_1 = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (k - 1) * ms_error + k * (ms_cols - ms_error) / n),
           icc_k = (ms_rows - ms_error) / (ms_rows + (ms_cols - ms_error) / n)))
}
#
# range of the ratings across the three prompt versions (per deck)
prompt_range <- function(d, cols){
  apply(d[, cols], 1, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
}
#
# model-level score of a dimension from the ratings of the three prompt versions
# (columns of x): each prompt version is standardized across the decks, the mean
# of the three standardized ratings is rescaled with the mean and the population
# standard deviation of all ratings of the model and dimension, bounded to 1-7,
# and rounded to two decimals
# -Note: missing ratings (NA) are ignored. `round(x * 100) / 100` rounds halves
#        to even after scaling by 100 (as numpy does), which reproduces the
#        scores in the data we received exactly
model_score <- function(x){
  x <- as.matrix(x)
  z <- cbind((x[, 1] - mean(x[, 1], na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x[, 1], na.rm = TRUE),
             (x[, 2] - mean(x[, 2], na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x[, 2], na.rm = TRUE),
             (x[, 3] - mean(x[, 3], na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x[, 3], na.rm = TRUE))
  pooled <- as.vector(x)
  pooled_sd <- sqrt(mean((pooled - mean(pooled, na.rm = TRUE))^2, na.rm = TRUE))
  score <- mean(pooled, na.rm = TRUE) + pooled_sd * rowMeans(z, na.rm = TRUE)
  round(pmin(pmax(score, 1), 7) * 100) / 100
}
#
# text-based quality scores from the ratings of the three prompt versions:
# model-level scores, dimension scores (mean of the two model-level scores,
# rounded to two decimals), the four standardized dimension scores, and the
# text-based quality score (their mean), put together as a data frame
quality_scores <- function(d){
  res <- data.frame(
    ip_score_qwen = model_score(d[, c("ip_a_qwen", "ip_b_qwen", "ip_c_qwen")]),
    ip_score_mistral = model_score(d[, c("ip_a_mistral", "ip_b_mistral", "ip_c_mistral")]),
    hc_score_qwen = model_score(d[, c("hc_a_qwen", "hc_b_qwen", "hc_c_qwen")]),
    hc_score_mistral = model_score(d[, c("hc_a_mistral", "hc_b_mistral", "hc_c_mistral")]),
    co_score_qwen = model_score(d[, c("co_a_qwen", "co_b_qwen", "co_c_qwen")]),
    co_score_mistral = model_score(d[, c("co_a_mistral", "co_b_mistral", "co_c_mistral")]),
    ol_score_qwen = model_score(d[, c("ol_a_qwen", "ol_b_qwen", "ol_c_qwen")]),
    ol_score_mistral = model_score(d[, c("ol_a_mistral", "ol_b_mistral", "ol_c_mistral")]),
    oq_score_qwen = model_score(d[, c("oq_a_qwen", "oq_b_qwen", "oq_c_qwen")]),
    oq_score_mistral = model_score(d[, c("oq_a_mistral", "oq_b_mistral", "oq_c_mistral")])
  )
  res$ip_score <- round((res$ip_score_qwen + res$ip_score_mistral) / 2 * 100) / 100
  res$hc_score <- round((res$hc_score_qwen + res$hc_score_mistral) / 2 * 100) / 100
  res$co_score <- round((res$co_score_qwen + res$co_score_mistral) / 2 * 100) / 100
  res$ol_score <- round((res$ol_score_qwen + res$ol_score_mistral) / 2 * 100) / 100
  res$overall_quality <- round((res$oq_score_qwen + res$oq_score_mistral) / 2 * 100) / 100
  res$ip_z <- as.numeric(scale(res$ip_score))
  res$hc_z <- as.numeric(scale(res$hc_score))
  res$co_z <- as.numeric(scale(res$co_score))
  res$ol_z <- as.numeric(scale(res$ol_score))
  res$quality_score <- (res$ip_z + res$hc_z + res$co_z + res$ol_z) / 4
  return(res)
}
#
# median of the available ratings of a column (i.e., model, dimension, and prompt
# version) without the responses that did not contain a rating
available_median <- function(d, refusals, col){
  median(d[[col]][d$id %notin% refusals$id[refusals$col == col]])
}
#
# text-based quality score computed as simple means across the prompt versions
# and the two models (missing ratings are ignored), put together as a data frame
# with the four standardized dimension scores and their mean
quality_simple <- function(d){
  ip <- (rowMeans(d[, c("ip_a_qwen", "ip_b_qwen", "ip_c_qwen")], na.rm = TRUE) +
           rowMeans(d[, c("ip_a_mistral", "ip_b_mistral", "ip_c_mistral")], na.rm = TRUE)) / 2
  hc <- (rowMeans(d[, c("hc_a_qwen", "hc_b_qwen", "hc_c_qwen")], na.rm = TRUE) +
           rowMeans(d[, c("hc_a_mistral", "hc_b_mistral", "hc_c_mistral")], na.rm = TRUE)) / 2
  co <- (rowMeans(d[, c("co_a_qwen", "co_b_qwen", "co_c_qwen")], na.rm = TRUE) +
           rowMeans(d[, c("co_a_mistral", "co_b_mistral", "co_c_mistral")], na.rm = TRUE)) / 2
  ol <- (rowMeans(d[, c("ol_a_qwen", "ol_b_qwen", "ol_c_qwen")], na.rm = TRUE) +
           rowMeans(d[, c("ol_a_mistral", "ol_b_mistral", "ol_c_mistral")], na.rm = TRUE)) / 2
  res <- data.frame(ip_z = as.numeric(scale(ip)), hc_z = as.numeric(scale(hc)),
                    co_z = as.numeric(scale(co)), ol_z = as.numeric(scale(ol)))
  res$quality_score <- (res$ip_z + res$hc_z + res$co_z + res$ol_z) / 4
  return(res)
}
#
# format a correlation (r and its 95% CI) for a table
cor_str <- function(x, y){
  res <- cor.test(x, y)
  paste0(weights::rd(res$estimate, 3), " [", weights::rd(res$conf.int[1], 3), ", ",
         weights::rd(res$conf.int[2], 3), "]")
}
#
# extract GLM results and put the results together as a table
glm_tbl <- function(model, coef_digits = 2, coef_bold = TRUE, p_threshold = 0.05, ...){
  # extract model parameters
  if("tobit" %in% class(model)){ # tobit model -> broom::tidy does not work
    res <- parameters::model_parameters(model)
    res <- res[c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "z", "p")]
    names(res) <- c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")
    # res[] <- lapply(res, function(x) { attributes(x) <- NULL; x })
  } else {
    res <- broom::tidy(model)
  }
  pvals <- res$p.value
  res$estimate <- sprintf(paste0("%.", coef_digits, "f"), res$estimate)
  res$std.error <- sprintf("%.3f", res$std.error)
  res$statistic <- sprintf("%.2f", res$statistic)
  # format p value
  res$p.value <- ifelse(res$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p.value, 3))
  # make estimates bold if below critical p value
  if(coef_bold){
    res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
  }
  # bind R2 and Adj. R2 to model parameters
  r2 <- performance::r2(model) # extract R2
  end <- nrow(res) + seq_len(length(r2))
  res[end,"term"] <- names(r2)
  res[end,"estimate"] <- weights::rd(unlist(r2), digits = 3)
  # return result
  return(res)
}
#
# repeat the column headers of a table above each group of rows (except the
# first), so that the headers are visible for every part of a long table
# -Note: the header rows of the HTML table are inserted before the rows with
#        the group labels (cf. `pack_rows`), without the stripes of the rows
repeat_header <- function(tbl){
  html <- as.character(tbl)
  header <- sub("(?s).*<thead>(.*)</thead>.*", "\\1", html, perl = TRUE)
  header <- gsub('<th style="', '<th style="box-shadow: none; ', header, fixed = TRUE)
  groups <- gregexpr('<tr grouplength=', html, fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  for(pos in rev(groups[-1])){
    html <- paste0(substr(html, 1, pos - 1), header, substr(html, pos, nchar(html)))
  }
  attributes(html) <- attributes(tbl)
  return(html)
}

3.1 Experimental pitch decks in the benchmark
Table 1 shows the median contrast, simplicity, and symmetry scores of the high and the low fluency versions of the 40 experimental pitch decks (the eight decks of Studies 1 and 2 and the 32 decks of Studies 3 and 4) and their percentile ranks among the 3,510 real pitch decks. The percentile rank of a pitch deck is the percentage of real pitch decks with a score at or below the score of the deck. For each measure, the table reports the median percentile rank and the range of the percentile ranks. Figure 1 shows the individual pitch decks.


Code
# percentile ranks among the real pitch decks (percentage of real decks with a

# long format: one row per deck and measure
d_decks |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(contrast, simplicity, symmetry), names_to = "measure", values_to = "score") |>
  mutate(pr = case_when(measure == "contrast" ~ contrast_pr,
                        measure == "simplicity" ~ simplicity_pr,
                        measure == "symmetry" ~ symmetry_pr)) -> d_decks_long

deck_summary <- function(d){
  d |> group_by(measure, fluency) |>
    summarize(median_score = weights::rd(median(score), 3),
              median_pr = sprintf('%.1f', median(pr)),
              range_pr = paste0(sprintf('%.0f', min(pr)), "–", sprintf('%.0f', max(pr))),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = fluency, values_from = c(median_score, median_pr, range_pr)) |>
    select(measure, median_score_HF, median_pr_HF, range_pr_HF, median_score_LF, median_pr_LF, range_pr_LF)
}

      align = "lcccccc") |>

title: Deck Benchmarking
section: 3.2 Text-based substantive quality of the real pitch decks
text:
3.2 Text-based substantive quality of the real pitch decks
To maintain confidentiality, we provided the VC firm with a computational pipeline that ran entirely within the firm’s environment, on the same pitch decks as the benchmarking study. The pipeline rendered the slides as images and extracted their text with the vision-language model GLM-OCR. A named-entity recognition procedure (spaCy) then replaced company names, founder names, and locations with placeholders (e.g., “[ORG]” or “[PERSON]”) to limit the recognition of known startups. Two open-weight LLMs from different developers, Qwen 3.5 (Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, Alibaba) and Mistral 3 Large (Mistral-Large-3-675B-Instruct-2512, Mistral AI), rated the anonymized text of each deck on 1–7 scales. The scales covered the four quality dimensions of our experiments (organizational capital, human capital, commercialization opportunity, and organizational legitimacy) and an overall quality rating, and their anchors described the evidence associated with low, intermediate, and high ratings. Since the models received the text only, the visual formatting of the slides was not part of their input. Each model rated each dimension with three meaning-preserving versions of the prompt (a temperature of 0 and a single integer as output), which results in 105,300 ratings (3,510 decks × 5 dimensions × 3 prompt versions × 2 models). Section 5 shows the three versions of each prompt.
For each deck, dimension, and model, the three ratings (one per prompt version) are combined into a model-level score, and the dimension score is the mean of the two model-level scores.1 The text-based quality score is the mean of the four standardized dimension scores (i.e., without overall quality). Correspondingly, the image-based fluency score is the mean of the standardized contrast, simplicity, and symmetry scores.
Note that 526 of the 105,300 archived responses (0.5%) did not contain a rating (“I cannot determine”). In the data we received, each of these responses was replaced by the median of the available ratings of the same model, dimension, and prompt version (a rating of 3 or 4). Section 3.6 shows that the results do not depend on these responses or on how the ratings are combined.
Table 2 shows the reliability of the ratings. The agreement across the three prompt versions is the ICC(2,1) of the three ratings per deck (separately for each model and dimension). The agreement between the two models is the quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ of the two rounded model-level scores. The prompt sensitivity is the percentage of decks whose three ratings differ by 2 or more points, separately for each model and for either of the two models.
Table 3 gives a descriptive overview of the benchmark data. The pitch decks were submitted to the VC firm between 2015 and 2023.


Code
# agreement across the three prompt versions (ICC(2,1)), per dimension and model
icc_prompts <- c(
  icc_2(d[, c("ip_a_qwen", "ip_b_qwen", "ip_c_qwen")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("ip_a_mistral", "ip_b_mistral", "ip_c_mistral")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("hc_a_qwen", "hc_b_qwen", "hc_c_qwen")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("hc_a_mistral", "hc_b_mistral", "hc_c_mistral")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("co_a_qwen", "co_b_qwen", "co_c_qwen")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("co_a_mistral", "co_b_mistral", "co_c_mistral")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("ol_a_qwen", "ol_b_qwen", "ol_c_qwen")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("ol_a_mistral", "ol_b_mistral", "ol_c_mistral")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("oq_a_qwen", "oq_b_qwen", "oq_c_qwen")])[["icc_1"]],
  icc_2(d[, c("oq_a_mistral", "oq_b_mistral", "oq_c_mistral")])[["icc_1"]]
)
# agreement between the models (quadratic-weighted kappa of the rounded model-level scores)
kappa_models <- c(
  irr::kappa2(cbind(round(d$ip_score_qwen), round(d$ip_score_mistral)), weight = "squared")$value,
  irr::kappa2(cbind(round(d$hc_score_qwen), round(d$hc_score_mistral)), weight = "squared")$value,
  irr::kappa2(cbind(round(d$co_score_qwen), round(d$co_score_mistral)), weight = "squared")$value,
  irr::kappa2(cbind(round(d$ol_score_qwen), round(d$ol_score_mistral)), weight = "squared")$value,
  irr::kappa2(cbind(round(d$oq_score_qwen), round(d$oq_score_mistral)), weight = "squared")$value
)
# range of the three ratings per deck, per dimension and model
range_ip_qwen <- prompt_range(d, c("ip_a_qwen", "ip_b_qwen", "ip_c_qwen"))
range_ip_mistral <- prompt_range(d, c("ip_a_mistral", "ip_b_mistral", "ip_c_mistral"))
range_hc_qwen <- prompt_range(d, c("hc_a_qwen", "hc_b_qwen", "hc_c_qwen"))
range_hc_mistral <- prompt_range(d, c("hc_a_mistral", "hc_b_mistral", "hc_c_mistral"))
range_co_qwen <- prompt_range(d, c("co_a_qwen", "co_b_qwen", "co_c_qwen"))
range_co_mistral <- prompt_range(d, c("co_a_mistral", "co_b_mistral", "co_c_mistral"))
range_ol_qwen <- prompt_range(d, c("ol_a_qwen", "ol_b_qwen", "ol_c_qwen"))
range_ol_mistral <- prompt_range(d, c("ol_a_mistral", "ol_b_mistral", "ol_c_mistral"))
range_oq_qwen <- prompt_range(d, c("oq_a_qwen", "oq_b_qwen", "oq_c_qwen"))
range_oq_mistral <- prompt_range(d, c("oq_a_mistral", "oq_b_mistral", "oq_c_mistral"))
# flip rates (in %)
flip_rates <- data.frame(
  qwen = c(mean(range_ip_qwen >= 2), mean(range_hc_qwen >= 2), mean(range_co_qwen >= 2),
           mean(range_ol_qwen >= 2), mean(range_oq_qwen >= 2)) * 100,
  mistral = c(mean(range_ip_mistral >= 2), mean(range_hc_mistral >= 2), mean(range_co_mistral >= 2),
              mean(range_ol_mistral >= 2), mean(range_oq_mistral >= 2)) * 100,
  either = c(mean(range_ip_qwen >= 2 | range_ip_mistral >= 2), mean(range_hc_qwen >= 2 | range_hc_mistral >= 2),
             mean(range_co_qwen >= 2 | range_co_mistral >= 2), mean(range_ol_qwen >= 2 | range_ol_mistral >= 2),
             mean(range_oq_qwen >= 2 | range_oq_mistral >= 2)) * 100
)

data.frame(dimension = c("Organizational capital", "Human capital", "Commercialization opportunity",
                         "Organizational legitimacy", "Overall quality"),
           icc_qwen = weights::rd(icc_prompts[c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9)], 3),
           icc_mistral = weights::rd(icc_prompts[c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10)], 3),
           kappa = weights::rd(kappa_models, 3),
           flip_qwen = sprintf('%.1f', flip_rates$qwen), flip_mistral = sprintf('%.1f', flip_rates$mistral),
           flip_either = sprintf('%.1f', flip_rates$either)) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("Dimension", "Qwen 3.5", "Mistral 3 Large", "Weighted κ", "Qwen 3.5", "Mistral 3 Large", "Either Model"),
      align = "lcccccc") |>

}

section: 3.6 Robustness: Construction of the text-based quality score
text:
3.6 Robustness: Construction of the text-based quality score
The analyses above use the construction of the scores described in Section 3.2, including the 526 responses without a rating that were replaced by the median of the available ratings. Table 9 shows the key statistics for two alternatives: the same construction with these responses treated as missing, and simple means across the three prompt versions and the two models (i.e., without standardization).


Code
# same construction with the responses that did not contain a rating treated
# as missing
d_na <- as.data.frame(d_text)
d_na[cbind(match(d_refusals$id, d_na$id), match(d_refusals$col, names(d_na)))] <- NA
q_construct_na <- quality_scores(d_na)
# simple means across the prompt versions and models
q_simple <- quality_simple(d_text)

# key statistics for a text-based quality score (and its human capital dimension)
robust_stats <- function(quality_score, hc_z){
  quality_top <- quality_score >= quantile(quality_score, .75)
  m <- glm(d$followon_funding ~ d$fluency_score + quality_score + d$funded_by_partner, family = binomial)
  c(r_quality = cor_str(d$fluency_score, quality_score),
    r_hc = cor_str(d$fluency_score, hc_z),
    below_median = sprintf('%.1f', mean(d$fluency_below_median[quality_top]) * 100),
    b_quality = sprintf('%.3f', coef(m)["quality_score"]),
    p_quality = weights::rd(coef(summary(m))["quality_score", "Pr(>|z|)"], 3))
}

data.frame(
  statistic = c("Correlation of the fluency score with the text-based quality score",
                "Correlation of the fluency score with human capital",
                "Top quality decks below the median fluency score (in %)",
                "Coefficient of the quality score for follow-on funding (joint model)",
                "p-value of this coefficient"),
  construct = robust_stats(d$quality_score, d$hc_z),
  construct_na = robust_stats(q_construct_na$quality_score, q_construct_na$hc_z),
  simple = robust_stats(q_simple$quality_score, q_simple$hc_z)
) |>
  kbl(col.names = c("", "Construction as in the Data", "Construction Without the Replaced Responses", "Simple Means"),
      align = "lccc", row.names = FALSE) |>

title: Study 1: Investor Engagement in the Field
text:
In our main study, we ran a field experiment in which we varied the visual fluency and the substantive quality of pitch decks of our two fictitious startups (Software: PerkSouq; Healthcare: Brachytix).
Specifically, we sent out a standardized email to 39,977 potential investors (24,961 for the software startup and 15,016 for healthcare startup), and tracked whether the potential investor clicks on the link to the pitch deck. Every investor who clicked the link within 21 days of receiving the email was potentially part of our sample (pending exclusion restrictions). All data that was recorded within 21 days after an investor clicked on the link to the pitch deck was considered for analysis.
Depending on their previous investment record, investors were matched to either the software startup or healthcare startup, then randomly assigned to one of the four experimental conditions. We pretested all the manipulations. We tracked whether an investor clicked on the link to the pitch deck, the cumulative time the pitch deck remained open, the proportion of pitch deck slides viewed (0–1), and whether there was a positive reaction to the email. A reaction was considered positive if a meeting appointment was scheduled over a link in the deck and / or an email reply has been sent that clearly demonstrated investor interest.1 Participants were not aware that they took part in a scientific study and that the startups were fictitious.
For more details, e.g., on the exclusion criteria that we used, see the corresponding AsPredicted preregistration listed in Table 1.

As this report is dynamically created with R and Quarto, we also report all code. However, for readability, code is hidden by default and only the relevant results are shown.

# Custom functions

# negate %in%
`%notin%` <- Negate(`%in%`)
#
# extract ANOVA results including eta squared and put the results together as a table
# -Note: needs the supernova library installed
anova_tbl <- function(formula, data, type = 3, ...){
  # perform ANOVA
  d <- supernova::supernova(lm(as.formula(deparse(formula)), data = data), type = type)$tbl
  # check whether ANOVA is univariate or factorial
  univariate <- all(d$term %in% c("Model", "Error", "Total"))
  # get rows of interest
  if(univariate) {
    effect_rows <- d$term %notin% c("Error", "Total")
  } else {
    effect_rows <- d$term %notin% c("Model", "Error", "Total")
  }
  # extract key parameters
  effect <- d$term[effect_rows]
  SS <- round(d$SS[effect_rows], 2)
  df <- d$df[effect_rows]
  df_res <- d$df[d$term == "Error"]
  statistic <- round(d$F[effect_rows], 2)
  pval <- ifelse(d$p[effect_rows] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$p[effect_rows], 3))
  eta <- ifelse(d$PRE[effect_rows] < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(d$PRE[effect_rows], 3))
  # construct return df
  return(data.frame(effect, SS, df, df_res, statistic, pval, eta))
}
# extract GLM results and put the results together as a table
glm_tbl <- function(model, coef_digits = 2, coef_bold = TRUE, p_threshold = 0.05, ...){
  # extract model parameters
  if("tobit" %in% class(model)){ # tobit model -> broom::tidy does not work
    res <- parameters::model_parameters(model)
    res <- res[c("Parameter", "Coefficient", "SE", "z", "p")]
    names(res) <- c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")
    # res[] <- lapply(res, function(x) { attributes(x) <- NULL; x })
  } else {
    res <- broom::tidy(model)
  }
  pvals <- res$p.value
  res$estimate <- sprintf(paste0("%.", coef_digits, "f"), res$estimate)
  res$std.error <- sprintf("%.3f", res$std.error)
  res$statistic <- sprintf("%.2f", res$statistic)
  # format p value
  res$p.value <- ifelse(res$p.value < .001, " < .001", weights::rd(res$p.value, 3))
  # make estimates bold if below critical p value
  if(coef_bold){
    res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$estimate[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$std.error[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$statistic[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
    res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold] <- paste0("<b>", res$p.value[pvals < p_threshold], "</b>")
  }
  # bind R2 and Adj. R2 to model parameters
  r2 <- performance::r2(model) # extract R2
  end <- nrow(res) + seq_len(length(r2))
  res[end,"term"] <- names(r2)
  res[end,"estimate"] <- weights::rd(unlist(r2), digits = 3)
  # return result
  return(res)
}

4.2 Opening duration, slide coverage
Table 5 shows the result of two factorial ANOVAs that model cumulative opening duration and slide coverage as a function of the visual fluency condition and the substantive quality condition. Note that type III sum of squares were used, and the proportional reduction in error is reported as effect size (ηp2 in the table).
Additionally, Table 6 shows the results of robustness check regressions in which we included investment experience, investor type, gender, and country as control variables in addition to fluency, quality, and their interaction (significant values with p < .05 are printed in boldface). In all analyses, we used effect coding for the two factors visual fluency and substantive quality. That is, for both variables, we coded low as -1 and high as +1.


Code

d$fluency <- as.factor(d$fluency)
d$quality <- as.factor(d$quality)

# relevel factor levels

d$fluency <- relevel(d$fluency, 'high')

# convert factor into effect coding
contrasts(d$fluency) <- contr.sum
contrasts(d$quality) <- contr.sum

# combine results
temp <- bind_rows(`Opening duration` = anova_tbl(duration ~ fluency * quality, d),
                  `Slide coverage` = anova_tbl(completion ~ fluency * quality, d),
                  .id = "Measure")

# keep only first occurrence of each measure

4.3 Positive reactions
A logistic regression model was estimated to analyze the effects of visual fluency, substantive quality, and their interaction on whether there was a positive reaction to the emails. Table 7 shows the result of this regression model, next to several robustness check models that included control variables (Table 7 (a)) and / or were specified as Tobit models (Table 7 (b)).
In all regressions, we used effect coding for the two factors visual fluency and substantive quality. That is, for both variables, we coded low as -1 and high as +1.

title: Study 1: Investor Engagement in the Field
text:
4.4 Percentage increases
To facilitate the interpretation of the results, we calculated the percentage increase in the dependent variables for the high level of visual fluency and substantive quality compared to the respective low level. Table 8 shows these percentage increases for the opening duration, slide coverage, and positive reactions.


Code
# calculate percentage increases based on marginal means
#
# compute marginal means using the `marginaleffects` package
#
# duration
m_dur <- aov(duration ~ fluency * quality, d)
mm_dur_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_dur, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_dur_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_dur, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
# completion
m_compl <- aov(completion ~ fluency * quality, d)
mm_compl_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_compl, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_compl_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_compl, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
# positive reactions
m_pos <- glm(positive ~ fluency * quality, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = d)
mm_pos_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_pos, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_pos_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_pos, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))

# compute effect sizes as percentage increases for high vs. low levels
#
# we use the formula: 100 * (high / low - 1)
# That is, we multiply by 100 to get the percentage increase and then
# subtract 1 to get the percentage increase relative to the low level.
#
# duration: fluency
perc_incr_dur_flu <- 100 * (mm_dur_flu$estimate[mm_dur_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_dur_flu$estimate[mm_dur_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# duration: quality
perc_incr_dur_qual <- 100 * (mm_dur_qual$estimate[mm_dur_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_dur_qual$estimate[mm_dur_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# completion: fluency
perc_incr_compl_flu <- 100 * (mm_compl_flu$estimate[mm_compl_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_compl_flu$estimate[mm_compl_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# completion: quality
perc_incr_compl_qual <- 100 * (mm_compl_qual$estimate[mm_compl_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_compl_qual$estimate[mm_compl_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# positive: fluency
perc_incr_pos_flu <- 100 * (mm_pos_flu$estimate[mm_pos_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_pos_flu$estimate[mm_pos_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# positive: quality
perc_incr_pos_qual <- 100 * (mm_pos_qual$estimate[mm_pos_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_pos_qual$estimate[mm_pos_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# create table
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Opening duration", "Slide coverage", "Positive reaction"),
  Fluency = c(sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_dur_flu), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_compl_flu), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_pos_flu)),
  Quality = c(sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_dur_qual), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_compl_qual), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_pos_qual))
) |> kbl() |> kable_styling()

5.2 Opening duration, slide coverage
Table 10 shows the result of two factorial ANOVAs that model cumulative opening duration and slide coverage as a function of the visual fluency condition and the substantive quality condition. title: Study 1: Investor Engagement in the Field
text:
5.4 Percentage increases
To facilitate the interpretation of the results, we calculated the percentage increase in the dependent variables for the high level of visual fluency and substantive quality compared to the respective low level. Table 13 shows these percentage increases for the opening duration, slide coverage, and positive reactions.


Code
# calculate percentage increases based on marginal means
#
# compute marginal means using the `marginaleffects` package
#
# duration
m_dur <- aov(duration ~ fluency * quality, d)
mm_dur_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_dur, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_dur_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_dur, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
# completion
m_compl <- aov(completion ~ fluency * quality, d)
mm_compl_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_compl, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_compl_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_compl, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
# positive reactions
m_pos <- glm(positive ~ fluency * quality, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = d)
mm_pos_flu <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_pos, by = c("fluency"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))
mm_pos_qual <- marginaleffects::predictions(m_pos, by = c("quality"), type = "response",
                   newdata = marginaleffects::datagrid(grid_type = "balanced"))

# compute effect sizes as percentage increases for high vs. low levels
#
# we use the formula: 100 * (high / low - 1)
# That is, we multiply by 100 to get the percentage increase and then
# subtract 1 to get the percentage increase relative to the low level.
#
# duration: fluency
perc_incr_dur_flu <- 100 * (mm_dur_flu$estimate[mm_dur_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_dur_flu$estimate[mm_dur_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# duration: quality
perc_incr_dur_qual <- 100 * (mm_dur_qual$estimate[mm_dur_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_dur_qual$estimate[mm_dur_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# completion: fluency
perc_incr_compl_flu <- 100 * (mm_compl_flu$estimate[mm_compl_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_compl_flu$estimate[mm_compl_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# completion: quality
perc_incr_compl_qual <- 100 * (mm_compl_qual$estimate[mm_compl_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_compl_qual$estimate[mm_compl_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# positive: fluency
perc_incr_pos_flu <- 100 * (mm_pos_flu$estimate[mm_pos_flu$fluency == "high"] / mm_pos_flu$estimate[mm_pos_flu$fluency == "low"] - 1)
# positive: quality
perc_incr_pos_qual <- 100 * (mm_pos_qual$estimate[mm_pos_qual$quality == "high"] / mm_pos_qual$estimate[mm_pos_qual$quality == "low"] - 1)

# create table
data.frame(
  Measure = c("Opening duration", "Slide coverage", "Positive reaction"),
  Fluency = c(sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_dur_flu), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_compl_flu), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_pos_flu)),
  Quality = c(sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_dur_qual), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_compl_qual), sprintf('%.1f%%', perc_incr_pos_qual))
) |> kbl() |> kable_styling()

# Software startup --------------------------------------------------
#
# prepare sankey data (the data is already loaded at the beginning of the script)
#
# create binary indicators for the different stages
sankey_soft |> mutate(
  `Sent mails` = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 1 ~ "Hard bounce",
    hard_bounce == 0 ~ "Delivered"
  ),
  Delivered = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 0 & is.na(date_first_click) ~ "Recipient did not open deck",
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_first_click) ~ "Recipient opened deck"
  ),
  `Recipient opened deck` = case_when(
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_first_click) & is.na(date_reply) ~ "Recipient did not reply",
    hard_bounce == 0 & !is.na(date_reply) ~ "Recipient replied"
  ),
  `Recipient replied` = case_when(
    positive == 0 ~ "Negative reply",
    positive == 1 ~ "Positive reply"
  ),
  Category = category,
  `Initial sample` = "Software<br>startup"
) -> sankey_soft

# make data long for sankey graph (for simplicity, just called `df`)
sankey_soft |> make_long(`Initial sample`, `Sent mails`, Delivered,
                         `Recipient opened deck`, `Recipient replied`,
                         Category) -> df

# add group_nodes (needed for calculation of group percentages later)
df |> mutate(
  group_node = case_when(
    node == "Hard bounce" | node == "Delivered" ~ "Software<br>startup",
    node == "Recipient did not open deck" | node == "Recipient opened deck" ~ "Delivered",
    node == "Recipient did not reply" | node == "Recipient replied" ~ "Recipient opened deck",
    node == "Negative reply" | node == "Positive reply" ~ "Recipient replied",
    node == "other" | node == "geography" | node == "no investments" | node == "stage" | node == "investment strategy" | node == "industry" | node == "no specific reason" ~ "Negative reply",
    node == "more info/clarification" | node == "meeting" | node == "formal application" | node == "updates" | node == "referral" ~ "Positive reply"
  )
) -> df

# add information about node N and group_node N and calculate percentages
df |>
  # count obs per node
  group_by(node) |> mutate(n = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # count obs per group_node
  group_by(group_node) |> mutate(n_group = ifelse(is.na(group_node), NA, n())) |>
  ungroup() |>
  # add percentages
  mutate(pct = n/n_group) -> df

# manually change order of nodes
df |> mutate(
  node = factor(node,
                levels = c("Software<br>startup",
                           "Hard bounce", "Delivered",
                           "Recipient did not open deck", "Recipient opened deck",
                           "Recipient did not reply", "Recipient replied",
                           "Negative reply", "Positive reply",
                           "other", "geography", "no investments", "stage", "investment strategy", "industry", "no specific reason",
                           "more info/clarification", "meeting", "formal application", "updates", "referral"
                )
  ),
  next_node = factor(next_node,
                levels = c("Software<br>startup",
                           "Hard bounce", "Delivered",
                           "Recipient did not open deck", "Recipient opened deck",
                           "Recipient did not reply", "Recipient replied",
                           "Negative reply", "Positive reply",
                           "other", "geography", "no investments", "stage", "investment strategy", "industry", "no specific reason",
                           "more info/clarification", "meeting", "formal application", "updates", "referral"
                )
  )
) -> df

# make sankey plot
#
# first change the data so that percentages are displayed in the node texts
df |> tidyr::drop_na(node) |>
  mutate(
    pct = ifelse(is.na(pct), 9999, pct), # dummy-replace NA with 9999, otherwise later ifelse does not work
    node_text = ifelse(
      # group_node and thus pct empty (here: 9999)
      pct == 9999,
      # yes, pct empty -> no percentages
      sprintf("<span style='font-weight:bold; font-family:Roboto Condensed'>%s</span><br><span style='color:gray25'>N = %s</span>",
                        node, scales::comma(n)),
      # no, pct not empty -> add percentages
      sprintf("<span style='font-weight:bold; font-family:Roboto Condensed'>%s</span><br><span style='color:gray25'>N = %s (%s%%)</span>",

# Helper functions and aesthetics

# pval function
pval <- function(p, stars = TRUE){
  if(stars){
    if(p < .001) return("***")
    if(p < .01) return("**")
    if(p < .05) return("*")
    if(p >= .05) return("NS")
  } else{
    scales::pvalue(p, prefix = c("p < ", "p = ", "p > "))
  }
}

# contrast: low quality: high vs. low fluency
p1 <- temp[5]
# contrast: high quality: high vs. low fluency
p2 <- temp[2]

# plot
positive_2 <- ggplot(d_health, aes(x=quality, y=positive, fill=fluency)) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", geom="bar", position=position_dodge(.91)) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, fun.args=list(mult=2), geom="errorbar", width=.08, linewidth=.9,
               position=position_dodge(.91)) +
  # cell means as labels inside the bars
  # --Note: the label of the smallest bar (low quality, low fluency) is placed
  #         lower, so that it does not overlap with the error bar

            aes(x = quality, y = ifelse(quality == "Low" & fluency == "Low", .004, .014),
                label = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * positive), group = fluency,
                color = fluency),
            position = position_dodge(.91), vjust = 0, size = 4.2,
            family = "Roboto Condensed", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("gray15", "white"), guide = "none") +
  my_style + my_theme + my_labs +
  labs(y="Positive reactions", title = "Healthcare startup", fill = "Fluency") +
  # theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0, .25)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse=TRUE)) +
  geom_signif(
    # p1
    xmin = c(0.775), xmax = c(1.225),
    y_position = .1425,
    textsize = 6,
    tip_length = .002,
    annotations = pval(p1),
    color = "gray45",
    vjust = .5
    ) +
  geom_signif(
    # p2
    xmin = c(1.775), xmax = c(2.225),
    y_position = .225,
    textsize = 6,
    tip_length = .002,
    annotations = pval(p2),
    color = "gray45",

title: Study 1: Investor Engagement in the Field
text:
7.1 Descriptives
After having applied the exclusion restrictions, there were 918 replies from the 4,445 investors in the analysis sample (20.65%) for the software startup. Of these 918 replies, 331 replies were positive (36.06% of replies).
For the healthcare startup, there were 733 replies from the 2,408 investors in the analysis sample (30.44%). Of these 733 replies, 236 replies were positive (32.20% of replies).
Table 14 shows a breakdown of the reply rate and the positive reactions per fluency and quality condition.


Code
# combine data
pos_given_reply_data <- bind_rows(list(
  Software = d_sw |> select(Fluency = fluency, Quality = quality, reply, positive_given_reply, investments, type, gender, location) |> mutate(n_mails = n_mails_sw),
  Healthcare = d_hc |> select(Fluency = fluency, Quality = quality, reply, positive_given_reply, investments, type, gender, location) |> mutate(n_mails = n_mails_hc)),
  .id = "Startup")
# convert Startup to factor, change order of levels
pos_given_reply_data$Startup <- factor(pos_given_reply_data$Startup, levels = c("Software", "Healthcare"))

# create table
pos_given_reply_data |>
  group_by(Startup, Fluency, Quality) |>
  summarize(
    `Clicks` = scales::comma(n()),
    `Replies ` = scales::comma(sum(reply)),
    `% Reply Rate ` = sprintf('%.2f', mean(reply)*100),
    `Pos. Reaction ` = scales::comma(sum(positive_given_reply, na.rm=T)),
    `% Pos. Reaction Rate ` = sprintf('%.2f', mean(positive_given_reply, na.rm=T)*100),
  ) |> kbl() |> kable_styling() |>
  row_spec(c(4), extra_css = "border-bottom: 1px solid")

text:
7.2 Results
We re-estimated the binary logit models (with control variables) reported in Table 7 and Table 12, now predicting whether there was a positive reaction to the emails conditional on investors having replied. Thus, for this analysis, the sample is a subset of the full sample (i.e., only investors who replied to the emails, N = 918 software startup, N = 733 healthcare startup). Table 15 shows the results of these models for the software and healthcare startup.


Code
d <- pos_given_reply_data

# 2 tables witch 2 colmuns each version

# convert conditions into factors
d$fluency <- as.factor(d$Fluency)
d$quality <- as.factor(d$Quality)

# relevel factor levels
d$quality <- relevel(d$quality, 'high')
d$fluency <- relevel(d$fluency, 'high')

# convert factor into effect coding
contrasts(d$fluency) <- contr.sum
contrasts(d$quality) <- contr.sum


# run regressions
glm_tbl(glm(positive_given_reply ~ fluency * quality + investments + type + gender + location, family = binomial(link = "logit"), d |> filter(Startup == "Software")), coef_digits = 3) -> temp_positive_given_reply_sw
glm_tbl(glm(positive_given_reply ~ fluency * quality + investments + type + gender + location, family = binomial(link = "logit"), d |> filter(Startup == "Healthcare")), coef_digits = 3) -> temp_positive_given_reply_hc

# put results together
temp <- bind_cols(temp_positive_given_reply_sw,
                  temp_positive_given_reply_hc[,-1]) |>
  mutate(term = c("Intercept", "Fluency", "Quality", "Investment experience",
               "Investor type [Venture Capital]", "Gender [Male]", "Country [Brazil]",
               "Country [Canada]", "Country [China]", "Country [France]",
               "Country [Germany]", "Country [India]", "Country [Israel]",
               "Country [Singapore]", "Country [United Kingdom]",
               "Fluency × Quality", "Tjur's R<sup>2</sup>"))

# change order of rows: put interaction after main effects
temp |> arrange(term %notin% c("Intercept", "Fluency", "Quality", "Fluency × Quality")) -> temp
# change column names
names(temp) <- c("", rep(c("Coeff.", "SE", "z", "p"), 2))

# create final table
temp |>
  kbl(escape = FALSE, align = "lcccccccc") |> kable_styling() |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "Software Startup" = 4, "Healthcare Startup" = 4)) |>
  row_spec(c(4,16), extra_css = "border-bottom: 1px solid")
